Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] M365/OWA look-alike phishing domains or poisoned resolution of legit M365 hosts · [LLM] ClickFix fake-update payload download provenance from CaptiveCrunch infra · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Entra ID device code authentication phishing (CaptiveCrunch) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] CornFlake RAT / ChocoShell stealer execution by known SHA256 · [LLM] CornFlake 'Cloud Sync Service' persistence from %AppData% (service/run-key/task watchdog) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] CaptiveCrunch / Storm-2945 C2 beacon to hardcoded Midnight Blizzard IPs · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
CaptiveCrunch / Storm-2945 C2 beacon to hardcoded Midnight Blizzard IPs AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound connections from any host to the six CornFlake/ChocoShell/FruitStone C2 IPs published for the CaptiveCrunch campaign. Because these are dedicated Storm-2945 infrastructure IPs, any egress to them is a high-confidence compromise signal regardless of the process involved. Rationale: Uses the six exact C2 IPs from the article's IOC block (corroborated by the Microsoft CaptiveCrunch blog); dedicated actor infra means any hit is near-zero-FP. IP-only match makes it portable across every network telemetry source. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wi-fi-pushes-fake.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A researcher/sandbox in the SOC intentionally detonating a CaptiveCrunch sample
  • Threat-intel enrichment or scanning service that actively probes the IPs from a scanner host
  • A shared hosting IP being re-provisioned to a benign tenant after the campaign (validate against current ThreatFox/OTX status)
  • VPN concentrator NAT collapsing multiple users behind one src_ip, obscuring the true infected host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("nessus.exe","vscan.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the beaconing host (InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine) and confirm whether it maps to CornFlake in %AppData% or an in-memory PowerShell (ChocoShell). 2) Contain: network-isolate the host in Defender, block all six IPs at the perimeter, and revoke/reset the user's M365 sessions and refresh tokens (token theft is a stated capability). 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for the malware hashes, 'Cloud Sync Service' persistence, and any other host that contacted the same IPs in the last 30 days.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("31.57.243.154","38.146.28.75","38.146.28.132","104.194.159.150","107.189.26.194","213.145.86.112")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP
| order by LastSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("31.57.243.154","38.146.28.75","38.146.28.132","104.194.159.150","107.189.26.194","213.145.86.112")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Connections=count(), Ports=make_set(DestinationPort) by SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by LastSeen desc

M365/OWA look-alike phishing domains or poisoned resolution of legit M365 hosts AIDelivery Medium
Hunts DNS/web traffic to the four Microsoft-365-spoofing domains used by CaptiveCrunch, and the DNS-manipulation twist where a legitimate Microsoft login hostname resolves to a Storm-2945 IP (the captive-portal DNS hijack). Distinguishes malicious captive-portal redirects from normal M365 usage. Rationale: Uses the four exact spoof domains from the IOC block plus a DNS-poisoning clause (legit Microsoft host answering with a Storm-2945 IP) that captures the article's core 'attackers manipulate DNS' behaviour on captive-portal networks. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html
ATT&CKT1557 T1566.002 T1584.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-registered marketing/tenant subdomain that happens to contain 'm365' or 'owa' strings (verify exact eTLD+1)
  • Security-awareness phishing-simulation vendor using look-alike domains for training
  • Corporate split-DNS/CDN fronting where a Microsoft host briefly resolves to an unusual but benign IP (validate the answer IP against the IOC list only)
  • Passive-DNS/threat-intel appliance resolving the IOC domains for enrichment
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has "phishtest" or RemoteUrl has "knowbe4")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the client actually connected (not just resolved) and identify the user + whether it occurred on a hotel/guest network segment. 2) Contain: force reauthentication and revoke sessions for the user, block the four domains and six IPs, and check for a subsequent ClickFix download on the host. 3) Hunt: search UrlClickEvents/proxy for credential submission to these domains and expand to other users who resolved the same domains.

CornFlake RAT / ChocoShell stealer execution by known SHA256 AIInstallation High
Detects execution or on-disk drop of the two CaptiveCrunch payload hashes — the Go-based CornFlake RAT and the ChocoShell PowerShell stealer. Unions process-execution and file-write telemetry so the drop is caught even when ChocoShell runs largely in-memory. Rationale: Uses the two exact SHA256 IOCs from the article (CornFlake 918fa5..., ChocoShell be9985...); a union across process + file telemetry catches both the RAT execution and the disk drop before an in-memory stealer erases the signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wi-fi-pushes-fake.html
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/reverse-engineering lab detonating the sample for analysis
  • Hash collision is not credible for SHA256 — effectively no benign FP for a true match
  • EDR/AV signature-testing host intentionally staging IOC files
  • Backup/DLP tooling reading the quarantined sample and re-hashing it (FileDrop rows only)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "malware-lab" and Account !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm it is a genuine execution (ProcessExec source) vs a quarantined drop, and capture the initiating parent (ClickFix chain vs %AppData% persistence). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, and revoke the user's M365/Entra tokens and browser sessions given the stated credential/token-theft capability. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same hashes, 'Cloud Sync Service' services/run-keys/tasks, and beaconing to the campaign C2 IPs.
let Hashes = dynamic(["918fa52ae45ed60ba7cc8bdc99c3cbe9ab92e0375ec31fc05d0d4513be11c593","be99857449d2856dd5a84e21c8a3d5e0e01456adb44062ddec5a6b4970d8d42c"]);
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in (Hashes) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Account=AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, CommandLine=ProcessCommandLine, Parent=InitiatingProcessFileName, Source="ProcessExec"),
  (DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in (Hashes) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Account=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, CommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Parent=InitiatingProcessParentFileName, Source="FileDrop")
| order by Timestamp desc
let Hashes = dynamic(["918fa52ae45ed60ba7cc8bdc99c3cbe9ab92e0375ec31fc05d0d4513be11c593","be99857449d2856dd5a84e21c8a3d5e0e01456adb44062ddec5a6b4970d8d42c"]);
union
  (ImProcessCreate | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in (Hashes) | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, FileName=ActingProcessName, SHA256, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, Source="ProcessExec"),
  (ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where TargetFileSHA256 in (Hashes) | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, FileName=TargetFileName, SHA256=TargetFileSHA256, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, Source="FileDrop")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: e3a6b1d9-92c4-4f77-a0e5-1c8b4d2f7a30

CornFlake 'Cloud Sync Service' persistence from %AppData% (service/run-key/task watchdog) AIInstallation High
Detects CornFlake's redundant persistence: a service/run-key/scheduled-task pointing into %AppData% and/or masquerading as 'Cloud Sync Service'. A time-bucketed correlation surfaces the watchdog behaviour where two or more distinct persistence mechanisms are (re)created on one host within minutes. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact masquerade string 'Cloud Sync Service' plus the %AppData% install path and the four named persistence mechanisms; the >=2-types-in-5-min bucket models the described watchdog that re-creates removed persistence. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://cyberinsider.com/microsoft-links-hotel-wi-fi-hacks-to-russian-midnight-blizzard-hackers/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1547.001 T1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry Endpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate cloud-sync agents (OneDrive/Dropbox/Box) that install per-user services/run-keys from AppData — filter by exact 'Cloud Sync Service' name and unsigned binary
  • Electron/Chromium auto-updaters staging helpers in %AppData%\Local
  • IT deployment tooling creating multiple startup entries during a software push (correlate with change-management)
  • Portable-app launchers registering run keys pointing at user-profile paths
Suppression filter
| where not (Actors has "OneDrive.exe" or Actors has "Dropbox.exe") and tostring(Details) !has "OneDrive"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the referenced binary's path, signer, and hash — a genuine CornFlake artifact is unsigned in %AppData% and named to impersonate a Windows component. 2) Contain: isolate the host, then remove ALL persistence types simultaneously (service + run key + task) because the watchdog restores any single removal; kill the running RAT/watchdog process first. 3) Hunt: verify the referenced hash against the campaign IOCs, and look for the same 'Cloud Sync Service' name and %AppData% path on other hosts.
let win = 5m;
union
  (DeviceRegistryEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated") | where RegistryKey has_any (@"\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\CurrentControlSet\Services") | where RegistryValueData has "AppData" or RegistryValueData has "Cloud Sync Service" or RegistryValueName has "Cloud Sync Service" | extend PersistType=iff(RegistryKey has "\\Run","RunKey","Service"), Detail=strcat(RegistryValueName," -> ",RegistryValueData), Actor=InitiatingProcessFileName),
  (DeviceEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where ActionType == "ScheduledTaskCreated" | where tostring(AdditionalFields) has "AppData" or tostring(AdditionalFields) has "Cloud Sync Service" | extend PersistType="ScheduledTask", Detail=tostring(AdditionalFields), Actor=InitiatingProcessFileName)
| where Actor !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Types=make_set(PersistType), Details=make_set(Detail), Actors=make_set(Actor) by DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, win)
| where array_length(Types) >= 2 or tostring(Details) has "Cloud Sync Service"
| order by LastSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 7045
| where ServiceName has "Cloud Sync" or ServiceFileName has "AppData"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceStartType, ServiceType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Entra ID device code authentication phishing (CaptiveCrunch) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts successful Entra ID device-code sign-ins — the auth flow Storm-2945 abuses via captive-portal device-code phishing pages. Surfaces the app, source IP/ASN and device trust so analysts can spot codes redeemed from hospitality/guest networks or unmanaged devices. Rationale: Targets the article's 'device code phishing pages that abuse Microsoft Entra ID authentication flows'; device-code success is rare in most tenants, and projecting ASN/IP/trustType lets analysts flag redemptions from hotel/guest networks. Datadog/Falcon/Splunk left blank because this telemetry lives in Entra sign-in logs not shipped to those platforms in most tenants. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard/
ATT&CKT1621 T1528
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code onboarding of smart-TVs, conference-room devices, IoT and CLI tools (az login --use-device-code)
  • Developers authenticating via device code for headless/SSH sessions
  • Legacy line-of-business apps that rely on device-code flow by design
  • Road-warriors legitimately authenticating from hotel Wi-Fi during travel
Suppression filter
| where AppDisplayName !in ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell") and UserAgent !has "azure-cli"
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify with the user whether they initiated a device-code login; cross-check the source IP/ASN against known hospitality ranges and whether the device is managed. 2) Contain: if unrecognised, revoke the user's refresh tokens and sessions, require re-registration for MFA/passkey, and disable device-code flow via Conditional Access if not required. 3) Hunt: pull all subsequent sign-ins/token use for that account from new IPs and check the endpoint for CornFlake/ChocoShell artifacts and C2 beacons.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| where ErrorCode == 0
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, DeviceTrustType, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, ConditionalAccessStatus
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| where ResultType == 0
| extend TrustType = tostring(DeviceDetail.trustType)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, AutonomousSystemNumber, TrustType, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, ConditionalAccessStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ClickFix fake-update payload download provenance from CaptiveCrunch infra AIDelivery Medium
Detects executables/scripts/APKs written to disk whose download provenance (origin IP or referrer URL) is CaptiveCrunch infrastructure — the ClickFix fake browser/OS-update delivery step. Pivots on file mark-of-the-web origin rather than the network connection or hash, catching first-seen payloads before their hash is known. Rationale: Combines the file-type set expected from ClickFix fake-update lures (exe/msi/apk/ps1/hta) with the article's exact origin IPs and spoof domains via mark-of-the-web provenance (FileOriginIP/FileOriginUrl); a genuinely distinct pivot from the hash and network UCs. Sigma/Datadog/Falcon left blank — download provenance is an XDR-specific field not carried in Sysmon/FDR. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wi-fi-pushes-fake.html
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign file coincidentally downloaded from an IP later re-provisioned to another tenant (validate IOC currency)
  • Passive-DNS/sandbox appliance fetching payloads from the IOC domains for analysis
  • Proxy re-writing FileOriginUrl such that the referrer is preserved but the file is benign (rare with these specific IOC hosts)
  • Security team red-team replaying the ClickFix lure in a lab
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "malware-lab" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file executed (correlate SHA256 to DeviceProcessEvents) and whether the download occurred on a hotel/guest network. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the dropped file, and revoke the user's M365/Entra sessions. 3) Hunt: pivot the dropped SHA256 across the fleet, look for 'Cloud Sync Service' persistence and C2 beacons to the six IPs, and check whether an APK variant targeted the user's mobile device.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".msi" or FileName endswith ".apk" or FileName endswith ".ps1" or FileName endswith ".hta"
| where FileOriginIP in ("31.57.243.154","38.146.28.75","38.146.28.132","104.194.159.150","107.189.26.194","213.145.86.112")
   or FileOriginUrl has_any ("ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com","m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com")
   or FileOriginReferrerUrl has_any ("ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com","m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, FileOriginIP, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("31.57.243.154","38.146.28.75","38.146.28.132","104.194.159.150","107.189.26.194","213.145.86.112")
   or Url has_any ("ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com","m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com")
| where Url has_any (".exe",".msi",".apk",".ps1",".hta") or FileName has_any (".exe",".msi",".apk",".ps1",".hta")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, DstIpAddr, FileName, HttpUserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("918fa52ae45ed60ba7cc8bdc99c3cbe9ab92e0375ec31fc05d0d4513be11c593", "be99857449d2856dd5a84e21c8a3d5e0e01456adb44062ddec5a6b4970d8d42c") or SHA1 in~ ("918fa52ae45ed60ba7cc8bdc99c3cbe9ab92e0375ec31fc05d0d4513be11c593", "be99857449d2856dd5a84e21c8a3d5e0e01456adb44062ddec5a6b4970d8d42c") or MD5 in~ ("918fa52ae45ed60ba7cc8bdc99c3cbe9ab92e0375ec31fc05d0d4513be11c593", "be99857449d2856dd5a84e21c8a3d5e0e01456adb44062ddec5a6b4970d8d42c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("918fa52ae45ed60ba7cc8bdc99c3cbe9ab92e0375ec31fc05d0d4513be11c593", "be99857449d2856dd5a84e21c8a3d5e0e01456adb44062ddec5a6b4970d8d42c") or SHA1 in~ ("918fa52ae45ed60ba7cc8bdc99c3cbe9ab92e0375ec31fc05d0d4513be11c593", "be99857449d2856dd5a84e21c8a3d5e0e01456adb44062ddec5a6b4970d8d42c") or MD5 in~ ("918fa52ae45ed60ba7cc8bdc99c3cbe9ab92e0375ec31fc05d0d4513be11c593", "be99857449d2856dd5a84e21c8a3d5e0e01456adb44062ddec5a6b4970d8d42c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["918fa52ae45ed60ba7cc8bdc99c3cbe9ab92e0375ec31fc05d0d4513be11c593", "be99857449d2856dd5a84e21c8a3d5e0e01456adb44062ddec5a6b4970d8d42c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Silver Pass-ta-key: non-Chrome process deletes/tampers Chrome passkey_enclave_state to force re-onboarding
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Golden Pass-ta-key: non-Chrome process reads chrome.exe memory to scrape the security domain secret · [LLM] Pass-ta-key: non-Chrome process accessing Google passkey credential store (LevelDB + enclave state)
Silver Pass-ta-key: non-Chrome process deletes/tampers Chrome passkey_enclave_state to force re-onboarding AIInstallation High
Hunts an unprivileged process (other than chrome.exe / Google updater) deleting, renaming, or modifying Chrome's local passkey state file `passkey_enclave_state`, the exact precondition Unit 42's Silver Pass-ta-key uses to force Chrome to re-register so the attacker can enroll their own user-verification key. Article-specific because it keys on the named FIDO enclave state file under the Chrome User Data profile, not generic file deletion. Rationale: Keys on the exact named local FIDO state file `passkey_enclave_state` under `\Google\Chrome\User Data\` that Unit 42 says must be deleted/invalidated to trigger Silver Pass-ta-key re-onboarding; only Chrome itself and the Google updater legitimately touch this file, so a non-Chrome writer is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication-security-risks/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/google-synced-passkey-malware-attack/
ATT&CKT1556 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Chrome profile reset / corruption repair performed by the user deleting the profile folder via explorer.exe
  • Endpoint backup or migration tooling (e.g. profile-sync utilities) copying/removing the User Data directory
  • Antivirus/EDR quarantine action removing files inside the Chrome profile
  • Disk-cleanup or CCleaner-style tools purging browser profile artifacts
  • IT reimaging scripts wiping %LocalAppData%\Google\Chrome
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","ccleaner.exe","backup.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcess (path, SHA256, signer) that deleted/modified passkey_enclave_state; confirm it is not chrome.exe/Google updater and check whether the user was actively resetting Chrome. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block/hash-ban the offending binary, and force the user to re-enroll passkeys from a clean device and review recent logins to passkey-protected accounts (eBay, Google, etc.). 3) Hunt: on the same host look for a follow-on process reading chrome.exe memory (Golden) or opening Sync Data\LevelDB, and check Google account for a newly registered device/verification key.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "passkey_enclave_state"
| where ActionType in ("FileDeleted","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","GoogleUpdateComRegisterShell64.exe","updater.exe","elevation_service.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, ActionType, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "passkey_enclave_state"
| where EventType in ("FileDeleted","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\"
| where ActingProcessName !has "chrome.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "GoogleUpdate" and ActingProcessName !has "updater.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Golden Pass-ta-key: non-Chrome process reads chrome.exe memory to scrape the security domain secret AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a foreign process opening or reading the memory of chrome.exe, the technique Unit 42's Golden Pass-ta-key uses to extract the security-domain-secret (SDS) master key that decrypts all synced passkeys after forcing a re-registration. Article-specific because it targets browser-process memory access to chrome.exe (not LSASS) — the only place the SDS transiently lives after Google removed it from the FIDO log. Rationale: Unit 42 states the SDS master key 'remains accessible in Chrome's process memory' and can be extracted 'directly from memory' after a forced re-registration; a non-browser process opening chrome.exe with read/VM-read access (GrantedAccess masks) is the observable for that scrape. Marked hunting due to legitimate memory access by AV/crash handlers. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication-security-risks/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1003
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint AV/EDR (MsMpEng.exe, MsSense.exe) scanning or monitoring browser memory
  • Chrome's own crashpad_handler.exe collecting a crash minidump of chrome.exe
  • Browser management / DLP agents that inspect browser memory
  • Performance/telemetry tools (e.g. Sysinternals procdump run by an admin) dumping chrome.exe
  • Enterprise password-manager browser integrations reading browser state
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("procdump.exe","procdump64.exe","taskmgr.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("administrator")) and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SourceImage/InitiatingProcess (path, signer, SHA256, integrity level) and confirm it is not a known AV/crash/DLP agent; note the GrantedAccess mask (read/VM_READ is suspicious). 2) Contain: isolate host, capture a memory image before reboot, hash-ban the process, and treat all Google-synced passkeys as compromised — the SDS cannot be rotated, so force passkey re-creation on affected accounts. 3) Hunt: correlate with a preceding passkey_enclave_state deletion (Silver) on the same host and outbound transfer of Sync Data\LevelDB; review Google account device list for rogue enrollments.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("OpenProcessApiCall","ReadProcessMemoryApiCall")
| where FileName =~ "chrome.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","crashpad_handler.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","updater.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, TargetProcess=FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("OpenProcessApiCall","ReadProcessMemoryApiCall")
| where FileName =~ "chrome.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","crashpad_handler.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","updater.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, ActionType, TargetProcess=FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

detection:

`sysmon` EventCode=10 TargetImage="*\\chrome.exe" NOT (SourceImage IN ("*\\chrome.exe","*\\msedge.exe","*\\MsMpEng.exe","*\\MsSense.exe","*\\SenseIR.exe","*\\crashpad_handler.exe","*\\GoogleUpdate.exe")) GrantedAccess IN ("0x1010","0x1410","0x1438","0x143a","0x1fffff","0x1f1fff","0x1f3fff") | stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(GrantedAccess) as GrantedAccess by dest, user, SourceImage, TargetImage | sort - lastTime
Pass-ta-key: non-Chrome process accessing Google passkey credential store (LevelDB + enclave state) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a process other than Chrome opening, copying, or modifying the Google Password Manager passkey stores — `Sync Data\LevelDB` (WebauthnCredentialSpecifics records) and `passkey_enclave_state` (the TPM-wrapped device identity key) — under the Chrome User Data profile. Article-specific because these are the exact files Unit 42 abuses: the enclave key to sign forged assertions (Pass-ta-key) and the LevelDB records to recover private keys (Golden). Rationale: Targets the two exact stores Unit 42 names — `Sync Data\LevelDB` holding WebauthnCredentialSpecifics records and `passkey_enclave_state` holding the wrapped identity private key — under `\Google\Chrome\User Data\`; any non-Chrome process opening/copying these is the read side of Pass-ta-key signing and Golden decryption. Falcon FileOpenInfo is the strongest telemetry as it captures reads Defender/Sysmon do not. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication-security-risks/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/google-synced-passkey-malware-attack/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1606
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint backup/DLP agents enumerating the Chrome profile directory
  • Antivirus/EDR on-access scanning of the LevelDB files
  • Browser profile migration or enterprise browser-management tooling
  • Indexing/search services (e.g. Windows Search) touching profile files
  • Chrome update/repair helper processes not covered by the allowlist
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SearchIndexer.exe","backup.exe","OneDrive.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the accessing process (signer, SHA256, parent, cmdline) and whether it read `passkey_enclave_state` (assertion forging) vs `Sync Data\LevelDB` (record theft); confirm it is not backup/AV. 2) Contain: isolate host, hash-ban the binary, and treat synced passkeys as compromised — force re-enrollment and audit the Google account device/key list. 3) Hunt: pivot to whether the same process also read chrome.exe memory (Golden SDS scrape) or deleted the enclave state (Silver), and look for exfil of the copied LevelDB off-host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "passkey_enclave_state") or (FolderPath has @"\Sync Data\LevelDB")
| where FolderPath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\"
| where ActionType in ("FileAccessed","FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","GoogleUpdateComRegisterShell64.exe","updater.exe","elevation_service.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFileName =~ "passkey_enclave_state") or (TargetFilePath has @"\Sync Data\LevelDB")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\"
| where EventType in ("FileAccessed","FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName !has "chrome.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "GoogleUpdate" and ActingProcessName !has "updater.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Chrome Process Accessing Google Passkey Credential Store
id: c41a7e58-9b2d-4d6a-8f0e-2b9d6c3a71ef
description: Detects a process other than Chrome/Google updater accessing the Google Password Manager passkey stores (Sync Data\LevelDB or passkey_enclave_state) under the Chrome User Data profile, per Unit 42 Pass-ta-key / Golden Pass-ta-key credential recovery.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication-security-risks/
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-pass-ta-key-attacks-let-malware-hijack-google-synced-passkeys/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:
  - attack.t1555.003
  - attack.t1606
logsource:
  category: file_access
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_store:
    - TargetFilename|endswith: '\passkey_enclave_state'
    - TargetFilename|contains: '\Sync Data\LevelDB\'
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains: '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
  filter_main:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\GoogleUpdate.exe'
      - '\updater.exe'
      - '\elevation_service.exe'
  condition: selection_store and selection_path and not filter_main
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\\passkey_enclave_state OR *\\Sync\ Data\\LevelDB\\* OR *\\Sync Data\\LevelDB\\*)) @TargetFilename:(*\\Google\\Chrome\\User\ Data\\* OR *\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\*) -@Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\GoogleUpdate.exe OR *\\updater.exe)
#event_simpleName=/^(FileOpenInfo|FileWritten)$/ TargetFileName=/\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\/i
| TargetFileName=/(passkey_enclave_state$|\\Sync Data\\LevelDB\\)/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|GoogleUpdate|updater|elevation_service)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="passkey_enclave_state" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Sync Data\\LevelDB\\*") AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\*" NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","updater.exe","elevation_service.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="passkey_enclave_state" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Sync Data\\LevelDB\\*") AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\*" NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","updater.exe","elevation_service.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | sort - lastTime
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Oracle audit: TO_DATE/TO_TIMESTAMP value carrying unescaped quotes or SQL tokens (Sequelize CVE-2026-69240) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-69240 quote-escape bypass at the database tier: SQL statements reaching an Oracle backend where a string value begins with TO_DATE/TO_TIMESTAMP yet also carries a concatenation operator (||), tautology (OR 1=1), inline comment (--), UNION, or a stacked-query DROP. Because Sequelize's escape() passes these values through unescaped when dialect='oracle', the injected fragment lands verbatim in the executed statement recorded in the Oracle unified audit trail. Rationale: Uses the exact bypass primitive named in the advisory (TO_DATE/TO_TIMESTAMP prefix) AND-ed with the concrete PoC tail (TO_DATE('0','Y')||'' OR 1=1--), so it fires on the injected fragment as it appears in Oracle audit SqlText rather than on benign date parsing. No CIM database datamodel exists, so a raw sourcetype search is used; Defender/Falcon carry no DB-query telemetry, hence empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v8fg-2rw7-q452 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-69240
ATT&CKT1190 T1565.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate parameterized reporting queries that concatenate TO_DATE(...) ranges in a WHERE clause
  • ETL / batch jobs building date-bounded predicates with TO_DATE and || string concatenation
  • DBA ad-hoc troubleshooting queries containing TO_DATE plus inline -- comments
  • ORM-generated views that legitimately embed TO_DATE(...)||column expressions
Suppression filter
| search NOT DBUSERNAME IN ("ETL_SVC","REPORT_SVC","BATCH_SVC")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full SqlText, DBUSERNAME, USERHOST and CLIENT_IP; confirm whether the statement originated from the application service account and whether the || / OR 1=1 / -- fragment is user-controlled input rather than static app SQL. 2) Contain: block the offending CLIENT_IP at the WAF/proxy and, if the app DB account is confirmed abused, rotate its credentials or temporarily disable it. 3) Hunt: enumerate every statement in the same audit session and adjacent sessions from that IP for UNION SELECT, UPDATE/DELETE/INSERT, or data-dictionary reads (ALL_TABLES, DBA_USERS) indicating exfiltration or tampering; confirm the app's Sequelize version.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName has "oracle" or SyslogMessage has "ORA" or SyslogMessage has_any ("TO_DATE","TO_TIMESTAMP")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("TO_DATE","TO_TIMESTAMP")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("||","OR 1=1","--","UNION","; DROP")
| project TimeGenerated, HostName, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
index=oracle (sourcetype="oracle:audit" OR sourcetype="oracle:audit:unified" OR sourcetype="oracle:xml:audit")
| eval sqltext=lower(coalesce(sql_text, SqlText, DBMSGTEXT, _raw))
| where like(sqltext,"%to_date%") OR like(sqltext,"%to_timestamp%")
| where like(sqltext,"%||%") OR like(sqltext,"%or 1=1%") OR like(sqltext,"%--%") OR like(sqltext,"% union %") OR like(sqltext,"%'; drop%")
| stats count as hits min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(sqltext) as samples by DBUSERNAME, USERHOST, CLIENT_IP
| sort - hits
HTTP request parameter carrying TO_DATE/TO_TIMESTAMP SQLi payload (Sequelize CVE-2026-69240) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound web requests whose query string or URL contains an Oracle TO_DATE/TO_TIMESTAMP function call combined with a concatenation operator, OR 1=1 tautology, comment sequence, or UNION — the delivery vector for CVE-2026-69240 before it reaches the Sequelize/Oracle backend. Targets edge telemetry (WAF, reverse proxy, IIS/Nginx access logs) so the payload is caught at initial access. Rationale: Keys on the article's literal delivery string http://host/path?firstName=TO_DATE('0','Y')||'' OR 1=1-- : TO_DATE/TO_TIMESTAMP prefix plus concat/tautology/comment after URL-decoding, matching the payload at the proxy/WAF before the DB. Defender has no inbound web-request query-string telemetry, so defender_kql is empty; no generic web source exists in the Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch scopes here. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v8fg-2rw7-q452 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-69240
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Burp, Acunetix, Nessus) probing the app with SQLi test strings
  • Scheduled penetration-test windows generating TO_DATE/UNION probe traffic
  • Legitimate date-range UI params that pass a TO_DATE-like literal plus a '--' separator in the value
  • Benign parameters that happen to contain the substring 'union' alongside a date token
Suppression filter
| search NOT (csUserAgent IN ("*Nessus*","*Acunetix*","*sqlmap*","*Burp*") OR cIP IN ("10.10.50.0/24"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode csUriQuery/uri_query, confirm the TO_DATE(...) fragment is followed by || / OR 1=1 / -- rather than a benign date, and check scStatus (200 vs 500) to gauge whether the backend accepted it. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF and add a virtual-patch rule rejecting param values matching TO_(DATE|TIMESTAMP)\(.*(\|\||--|OR 1=1). 3) Hunt: correlate the same cIP against Oracle audit trail for executed TO_DATE injection statements and confirm the target app is running Sequelize <=6.37.3 with dialect oracle.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| extend q = tolower(url_decode(csUriQuery))
| where q has_any ("to_date","to_timestamp")
| where q has_any ("||","or 1=1","--","union")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable Sequelize <=6.37.3 package present in node_modules (CVE-2026-69240 exposure) AIReconnaissance Low
Proactive discovery hunt that surfaces hosts and repos where the sequelize package is installed under node_modules, so analysts can inspect the version and Oracle-dialect config for CVE-2026-69240 exposure. This is an asset-inventory pivot for remediation, not an exploitation alert. Rationale: Article pins v6.37.3 (vuln < 6.37.4) with dialect oracle as the vulnerable condition; locating node_modules/sequelize/package.json across the estate builds the remediation asset list. File telemetry cannot read the version string, so this is Low-confidence inventory and there is no clean FP filter — analysts must open package.json to confirm <=6.37.3. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v8fg-2rw7-q452 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-69240
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts already patched to sequelize 6.37.4+ (same file path, fixed version)
  • Apps using a non-Oracle dialect (postgres/mysql/mssql) that are not exploitable
  • Dev/test/CI build agents with transient node_modules trees
  • Vendored or nested node_modules copies inside unrelated tooling
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the matched package.json (and the app's Sequelize dialect config) to confirm version <=6.37.3 AND dialect: 'oracle' — only that combination is exploitable. 2) Contain: upgrade the package to sequelize 6.37.4 (the fixed release) and redeploy; where immediate patching is impossible, front the endpoint with the WAF rule from the HTTP-payload UC. 3) Hunt: enumerate all repos/CI pipelines and other hosts returned by this query to build a complete exposure inventory and confirm none are internet-facing while unpatched.

| where FileName =~ "package.json"
| where FolderPath has "node_modules" and FolderPath has "sequelize"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

| where TargetFileName =~ "package.json"
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules" and TargetFilePath has "sequelize"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Oracle ORA- syntax-error spike correlated with TO_DATE/TO_TIMESTAMP requests (CVE-2026-69240 probing) AIExploitation Medium
Alerts when a single source/app instance generates a burst of Oracle ORA-00911 (invalid character), ORA-00903 (invalid table name), or ORA-01858 (non-numeric where numeric expected) errors within a short window — the noisy fingerprint of failed CVE-2026-69240 quote-bypass attempts as an attacker tunes the TO_DATE/TO_TIMESTAMP payload before a working injection lands. Rationale: Failed quote-bypass attempts against Sequelize's oracle escape() throw exactly these syntax/invalid-character errors (ORA-00911 from stray quotes, ORA-01858 from malformed TO_DATE args); a 5-in-10-minute burst from one IP/app instance is the tuning signature the reviewer described. Threshold + time-window correlation makes this alerting-tier and unsuitable for Sigma; DB error logs are not in Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch scope. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v8fg-2rw7-q452 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-69240
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Application bug pushing malformed user date input into TO_DATE producing ORA-01858 bursts
  • A misconfigured batch/ETL job with a date-format mismatch
  • Schema migration or deployment window generating transient invalid-identifier errors
  • Load-test or synthetic monitoring hammering an endpoint with bad parameters
Suppression filter
| search NOT DBUSERNAME IN ("ETL_SVC","BATCH_SVC","MIGRATION_SVC")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on the CLIENT_IP/DBUSERNAME in the burst and pull the corresponding statements from the Oracle audit trail — confirm the failing SQL contains TO_DATE/TO_TIMESTAMP with quote/concat fragments rather than an application data-format bug. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/proxy and watch for a follow-on successful injection (statement with the same fragment but no ORA- error). 3) Hunt: correlate the burst timestamps with web access logs (HTTP-payload UC) for the same client, and verify whether any statement in the session subsequently succeeded, indicating a working bypass.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ProcessName has "oracle" or SyslogMessage has "ORA-"
| extend OraCode = extract("(ORA-[0-9]{5})", 1, SyslogMessage)
| where OraCode in ("ORA-00911","ORA-00903","ORA-01858")
| summarize errcount=count(), codes=make_set(OraCode) by bin(TimeGenerated, 10m), HostName, Computer
| where errcount >= 5
| order by errcount desc
APPLICATION
index=oracle (sourcetype="oracle:alert" OR sourcetype="oracle:database:error" OR sourcetype="oracle:audit" OR sourcetype="oracle:audit:unified")
| rex field=_raw "(?<ora>ORA-\d{5})"
| where ora IN ("ORA-00911","ORA-00903","ORA-01858")
| bin _time span=10m
| stats count as errcount dc(ora) as distinctCodes values(ora) as errorCodes by _time, CLIENT_IP, DBUSERNAME
| where errcount >= 5
| sort - errcount

New DOUBLECUP ClickFix service hides malware in browser cache images

BleepingComputer
2026-08-03 15 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A new Russian loader-as-a-service named DOUBLECUP uses ClickFix attacks to hide malicious code in PNG images cached by victims' browsers, ultimately delivering CountLoader to Windows and macOS devices and a new remote access trojan named DeviceManager to Windows systems. [...]

DOUBLECUP stego payload carved from browser cache via findstr/certutil AIInstallation High
Hunts the DOUBLECUP ClickFix execution step where the pasted command searches the browser cache for a PNG matched by exact file size and uses findstr or certutil to recover and run the hidden first-stage payload. Article-specific because it pins the two named LOLBins to Chromium/Firefox cache directory tokens rather than generic certutil decode. Rationale: Ties the article's two explicitly named recovery binaries (findstr, certutil) to browser cache-storage tokens (Cache_Data for Chromium/Edge/Brave/Opera, cache2 for Firefox) — a combination legitimate admin usage almost never produces. Cross-checked against: • https://www.silentpush.com/blog/countloader/
ATT&CKT1027.003 T1140 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint DFIR/forensic tooling parsing browser cache with certutil
  • Developer using certutil to decode a base64 asset stored under a Cache_Data path
  • Security researcher manually carving a cached file
  • Automated browser-artifact backup script referencing cache2 folders
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("kape.exe","autopsy.exe","velociraptor.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the parent chain — a paste-run from explorer.exe/Run dialog or a browser child is the DOUBLECUP tell. Note the referenced cache file and its size. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture the cached PNG and any dropped in-memory child; block the DOUBLECUP domains/IPs at proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: search the same host for the follow-on public-IP lookup, blockchain RPC calls, and TXT-record DNS bursts (UC4/UC5) that indicate CountLoader/DeviceManager staged successfully.

DOUBLECUP ClickFix fake-CAPTCHA phishing domain contact (NetSuite/Odoo/HubSpot lures) AIDelivery High
Hunts hosts resolving or connecting to the DOUBLECUP ClickFix lure domains impersonating NetSuite, Odoo and HubSpot login pages, plus the service's licensing/staging IPs. This is the initial-access pivot before any payload runs, keyed on named article IOCs rather than generic phishing. Rationale: Uses the article's pre-extracted lure domains and the two campaign IPs (213.139.77.109 licensing panel, 66.29.148.143). Domains are single-purpose typosquats of SaaS logins, so a resolution is near-certain malicious. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-doublecup-clickfix-service-hides-malware-in-browser-cache-images/

DOUBLECUP dropper public-IPv4 lookup feeding per-victim payload decryption key AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the fileless second-stage dropper behaviour where a script/LOLBin process retrieves the victim's public IPv4 from an echo service and uses it to derive the AES key for the final encrypted payload. Article-specific in scoping the IP-echo lookup to non-browser interpreter processes rather than normal user browsing. Rationale: The article states the dropper 'retrieves the victim's public IPv4 address and uses it to create a decryption key'; the query surfaces that behaviour by scoping the canonical public-IP-echo services to script/LOLBin initiators (the echo endpoints are the real-world services the technique relies on, listed as the detection surface — not claimed as article-cited IOCs). Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-doublecup-clickfix-service-hides-malware-in-browser-cache-images/

DeviceManager RAT EtherHiding C2 resolution via Ethereum/Polygon RPC AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the DeviceManager RAT resolving its live C2 address from an Ethereum or Polygon smart contract (EtherHiding). Detection flags interpreter/LOLBin processes reaching public blockchain RPC providers — traffic that has no business originating from a scripted host process. Rationale: The article states DeviceManager 'uses EtherHiding to retrieve its current C2 address from an Ethereum or Polygon smart contract'; corroborated by public EtherHiding write-ups describing RSA-signed contract responses. Scoping the major public RPC providers to the Python RAT runtime / LOLBins isolates the malicious lookup from developer Web3 traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/minecraft-malware-loader-uses-rsa-signed/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-doublecup-clickfix-service-hides-malware-in-browser-cache-images/

1) Triage: confirm the host has no legitimate Web3 development role; inspect the process making the RPC call and any ABI-encoded eth_call payload. 2) Contain: isolate host, block the RPC endpoints for that host, snapshot memory for the Python RAT. 3) Hunt: extract the resolved C2 IP from the contract response and sweep the fleet for connections to it, plus TXT-record DNS activity (UC5).
