DeviceManager RAT DNS TXT-record tunnelling for C2 and system-info exfil AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the DeviceManager RAT's use of DNS A and TXT records to retrieve commands, pull payloads and exfiltrate collected host data. Detection is a per-host TXT-query volume/fan-out anomaly, correlated where possible with the Python runtime, rather than a static IOC. Rationale: The article states DeviceManager 'uses DNS A and TXT records to steal system information, retrieve commands to execute, download payloads, and send command output back'. TXT records are rare in normal user browsing, so a >50 TXT/hr or >30-distinct-name burst (Defender approximates via the Python runtime because its schema lacks a query-type column) is high-signal tunnelling. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-doublecup-clickfix-service-hides-malware-in-browser-cache-images/

  • Mail servers doing SPF/DKIM/DMARC TXT lookups at volume
  • Certificate ACME DNS-01 validation bursts
  • Security scanners enumerating TXT records
  • CDN/anti-spam appliances performing bulk DNS TXT checks
Suppression filter
| where Computer !in~ ("MAILGW01","MAILGW02") and ClientIP !in ("")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process generating the TXT queries and decode a sample of the query labels / TXT responses for base64 or hex chunks. 2) Contain: isolate host, block the parent DNS zone at the resolver, kill the Python RAT process. 3) Hunt: correlate with the EtherHiding RPC lookup (UC4) and the collected-host-data (machine GUID, SID, AV list) staging; sweep for the same second-level domain across other hosts.
DeviceEvents | where Timestamp > ago(1d) | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse" | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe") | summarize QueryCount = count(), DistinctDomains = dcount(RemoteUrl) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 1h) | where DistinctDomains > 30 | order by DistinctDomains desc
DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) | where QueryType == "TXT" | summarize TxtQueryCount = count(), DistinctNames = dcount(Name) by Computer, ClientIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) | where TxtQueryCount > 50 | order by TxtQueryCount desc
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest RequestType=/TXT/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(as=TxtCount)) | TxtCount > 50
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.record_type="TXT" by DNS.src _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | where count > 50 | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.record_type="TXT" by DNS.src _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | where count > 50 | sort - count
CountLoader mshta scheduled-task persistence (GoogleTaskSystem pattern) AIInstallation High
Hunts CountLoader's persistence step: a scheduled task that re-launches mshta against a C2/fallback domain on a recurring interval. Corroborated externally as a task named GoogleTaskSystem<version><GUID> running mshta every 30 minutes — this UC keys on schtasks /create invoking mshta and that name pattern. Rationale: The article states CountLoader 'establishes persistence through scheduled tasks'; Silent Push and McAfee corroborate the exact shape — a task named GoogleTaskSystem<ver><GUID> invoking mshta against a fallback domain every 30 minutes. schtasks /create + mshta is a rare, high-fidelity combination. Cross-checked against: • https://www.silentpush.com/blog/countloader/ • https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/sinkholing-countloader-insights-into-its-recent-campaign/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1218.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy LOB app installer registering an mshta-based task
  • Admin scheduling an .hta maintenance script
  • Software packaging tool that wraps an HTA
  • MDM/RMM creating tasks that reference mshta for a report
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","ccmexec.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full schtasks command line and the task's target URL/HTA; a random 9-char string or fallback domain confirms CountLoader. 2) Contain: delete the scheduled task, isolate host, block the referenced domain. 3) Hunt: search the endpoint for the preceding cache-carve / dropper chain (UC1/UC3) and for CountLoader's discovery of crypto wallets, browser extensions and Signal Desktop.
DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where AccountName !endswith "$" | where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" | where ProcessCommandLine has "/create" | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("mshta","GoogleTaskSystem") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine | order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where EventID == 4688 | where NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe" | where CommandLine has "/create" and CommandLine has_any ("mshta","GoogleTaskSystem") | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName | order by TimeGenerated desc
title: CountLoader mshta Scheduled-Task Persistence
id: 2f9d5a67-4c81-4b02-9e3a-8d7c1b6e0f42
description: schtasks /create registering a task that launches mshta, matching CountLoader persistence (GoogleTaskSystem naming)
references:
  - https://www.silentpush.com/blog/countloader/
  - https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/sinkholing-countloader-insights-into-its-recent-campaign/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.t1218.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '/create'
  payload:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'mshta'
      - 'GoogleTaskSystem'
  condition: selection and payload
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:(*/create* AND (*mshta* OR *GoogleTaskSystem*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i | regex("/create", field=CommandLine) | regex("(mshta|GoogleTaskSystem)", field=CommandLine) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*" AND (Processes.process="*mshta*" OR Processes.process="*GoogleTaskSystem*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*" AND (Processes.process="*mshta*" OR Processes.process="*GoogleTaskSystem*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
macOS CountLoader native-recon burst (system_profiler/ioreg/sw_vers) + LaunchAgent AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the macOS CountLoader variant that fingerprints the host with built-in utilities (sw_vers, system_profiler, ioreg) and beacons via curl before installing a LaunchAgent. Detection clusters multiple native recon tools spawned by one non-shell parent in a short window — the DOUBLECUP macOS staging signature. Rationale: The article states the recovered macOS CountLoader 'uses built-in utilities such as curl, sw_vers, system_profiler, and ioreg' and installs a LaunchAgent. Clustering >=2 of these native recon tools under one non-shell parent in 5 minutes is the malware's fingerprinting signature; Sentinel is left empty as it carries no clean macOS process telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-doublecup-clickfix-service-hides-malware-in-browser-cache-images/
ATT&CKT1082 T1543.001 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MDM/Jamf inventory runs invoking system_profiler + ioreg
  • Apple diagnostics / sysdiagnose collection
  • IT asset-management agents querying hardware info
  • Developer build scripts calling sw_vers for version gating
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("jamf","osqueryd","munki","sysdiagnose")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent binary spawning the recon tools — a Jamf/osquery agent is benign; an unsigned binary in a user temp/Downloads path is not. 2) Contain: isolate the Mac, quarantine the parent binary, check ~/Library/LaunchAgents for a new plist and remove it. 3) Hunt: review outbound curl connections from the same parent for the attacker C2, and sweep other Macs for the same LaunchAgent label.
DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where FileName in~ ("system_profiler","ioreg","sw_vers") | where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("system_profiler","ioreg","sw_vers") | summarize ReconTools = make_set(FileName), Cmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine), ToolCount = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, bin(Timestamp, 5m) | where ToolCount >= 2 | order by ToolCount desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceProcessEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where FileName in~ ("system_profiler","ioreg","sw_vers") | where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("system_profiler","ioreg","sw_vers") | summarize ReconTools = make_set(FileName), Cmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine), ToolCount = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m) | where ToolCount >= 2 | order by ToolCount desc
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(system_profiler|ioreg|sw_vers)$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName], function=count(as=ReconCount)) | ReconCount >= 2
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Processes.process_name) as recon_tools dc(Processes.process_name) as tool_count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("system_profiler","ioreg","sw_vers") by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where tool_count >= 2
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process_name) as recon_tools dc(Processes.process_name) as tool_count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("system_profiler","ioreg","sw_vers") by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where tool_count >= 2
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/

date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access

    category: file_access
    product: windows

    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

title: Scheduled Task Creation with Suspicious Image / Encoded Args

description: |

author: Clankerusecase

tags:
    - attack.t1053.005
    - attack.persistence
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_schtasks:
        Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
        CommandLine|contains: '/create'
    selection_payload:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'powershell'
            - 'cmd.exe'
            - 'rundll32'
            - '-enc'
            - 'FromBase64'
            - '\Users\Public'
            - '\AppData\'
    condition: selection_schtasks and selection_payload
falsepositives:
    - GPO-driven scheduled tasks, MDT/SCCM imaging
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake Xeno Executor installers are infecting unsuspecting Roblox players with malware that provides remote access and steals sensitive information. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Fake Xeno loader (xeno.exe) executed from archive/Downloads/Temp staging
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Fake Roblox Xeno script launcher pushes infostealer, RAT malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Java runtime (javaw.exe/jvm.dll) dropped to AppData by non-installer process · [LLM] Obfuscated decompiler.exe spawned by xeno.exe / javaw (second-stage masquerade) · [LLM] 'Display Calibration' Run key persistence pointing to AppData javaw/GameDVR
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Xeno RAT C2 egress to solthere.net / dynamic .xyz WebSocket from AppData Java · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Single process reading credential stores across 3+ browsers (stealer sweep) · [LLM] Exodus wallet app.asar tamper / SquirrelInteractive.bin drop by non-Exodus process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
Fake Xeno loader (xeno.exe) executed from archive/Downloads/Temp staging AIDelivery High
Hunts the first-stage Powercat/Xeno loader: a binary named xeno.exe launched from a ZIP/SFX extraction path or spawned by an archiver, rather than from an installed program directory. Xeno is never legitimate official software, so any xeno.exe running out of Downloads/Temp/AppData is the entry point of this infection chain. Rationale: Uses the article's named first-stage binary 'xeno.exe' plus the delivery mechanism (ZIP/SFX archives extracted then launched). Bitdefender confirms the install path %LOCALAPPDATA%\Xeno\workspace\cache\xeno.exe; the archive/Downloads staging path makes this the highest-fidelity single entry-point pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor • https://www.threatlocker.com/blog/powercat-malware-campaign-fake-game-cheats-deliver-infostealer-targeting-discord-roblox-and-crypto-wallets • https://hackread.com/microsoft-fake-xeno-roblox-utilities-windows-rat/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A player who legitimately downloaded a real Xeno Executor build from its GitHub/xeno.onl source and ran it from Downloads (still risky, but not this malware)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox from an extracted folder
  • A developer named their own unrelated tool xeno.exe and runs it from a project temp dir
  • Renamed-but-benign gaming utility extracted by 7-Zip
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe") and FolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 and compare to Bitdefender's IOC MD5 list; check whether the process subsequently touched %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java\jre\bin\javaw.exe or spawned decompiler.exe. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the xeno.exe/javaw process tree, and force-reset the user's Roblox, Discord, Microsoft and any crypto-wallet credentials from a clean device. 3) Hunt: pivot on DeviceFileEvents for %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\GameDVR JAR drops, the 'Display Calibration' Run key, and outbound solthere.net connections across the fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "xeno.exe"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Temp\")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winrar.exe","7zfm.exe","7zg.exe","7z.exe","explorer.exe","winzip32.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\xeno.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\") or ParentProcessName has_any ("winrar.exe","7zfm.exe","7zg.exe","7z.exe","explorer.exe","winzip32.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Fake Xeno Loader Executed from Archive or Download Staging
id: 9f1c2a4e-5b7d-4c2a-a1e3-7f0b9d6e12a4
description: Detects xeno.exe (Powercat first-stage loader) launched from Downloads/Temp or spawned by an archiver, matching the fake Roblox Xeno Executor campaign.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-roblox-xeno-script-launcher-pushes-infostealer-rat-malware/
  - https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith: '\xeno.exe'
  selection_ctx:
    - Image|contains:
        - '\Downloads\'
        - '\AppData\Local\Temp\'
        - '\Temp\'
    - ParentImage|endswith:
        - '\winrar.exe'
        - '\7zfm.exe'
        - '\7zg.exe'
        - '\explorer.exe'
  condition: selection_img and selection_ctx
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\xeno.exe OR *\Xeno.exe OR *\XENO.EXE) (@Image:(*\Downloads\* OR *\Temp\* OR *\AppData\Local\Temp\*) OR @ParentImage:(*\winrar.exe OR *\WinRAR.exe OR *\7zFM.exe OR *\7zG.exe OR *\explorer.exe OR *\Explorer.EXE))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\xeno\.exe$/i
| (regex("(?i)\\\\(Downloads|Temp)\\\\", field=ImageFileName) OR ParentBaseFileName=/(winrar|7zfm|7zg|7z|explorer)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="xeno.exe" AND (Processes.process_path="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winrar.exe","7zfm.exe","7zg.exe","7z.exe","explorer.exe","winzip32.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="xeno.exe" AND (Processes.process_path="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winrar.exe","7zfm.exe","7zg.exe","7z.exe","explorer.exe","winzip32.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Java runtime (javaw.exe/jvm.dll) dropped to AppData by non-installer process AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the loader's JRE provisioning step: the fake Xeno payload checks for a Java Runtime and, if absent, extracts a private JRE (instance.exe archive) to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java\jre\bin\javaw.exe. A java runtime being written under AppData/Temp by something other than an official Java installer is a strong multi-stage marker. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's 'checks for a Java Runtime Environment, and extracts one if necessary' step and Bitdefender's confirmed path %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java\jre\bin\javaw.exe (dropped from instance.exe). A JRE materialising in AppData without an installer parent is the deployment tell. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor
ATT&CKT1027 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable/embedded JRE shipped by legitimate apps (some game launchers, Ghidra, Burp, Minecraft launcher) unpacking javaw.exe to AppData
  • Corporate software distribution tool staging a private JRE outside msiexec
  • A developer extracting a JDK zip into a Temp folder
  • Minecraft's own bundled runtime under AppData\Roaming\.minecraft\runtime (tune path exclusion)
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has @"\AppData\Roaming\.minecraft\runtime\" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the parent process — if xeno.exe or an unsigned binary from Downloads/Temp dropped the JRE, treat as malicious; benign if parent is a signed installer/launcher. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill javaw.exe running from AppData\Local\Java, and quarantine the dropping process. 3) Hunt: look for decompiler.exe execution, GameDVR-folder JAR (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\GameDVR), the 'Display Calibration' Run key, and solthere.net egress on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("javaw.exe","java.exe","jvm.dll")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Java\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Xeno\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","javasetup.exe","jdk-installer.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("javaw.exe","java.exe","jvm.dll")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Java\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Xeno\")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","javasetup.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Obfuscated decompiler.exe spawned by xeno.exe / javaw (second-stage masquerade) AIInstallation High
Hunts the second stage: the loader launches an obfuscated Java payload disguised as decompiler.exe, which performs environment checks, registers the victim to C2, and pulls the final RAT. A process named decompiler.exe whose parent is xeno.exe or javaw.exe running from AppData is a direct masquerade IOC for this campaign. Rationale: The article explicitly names 'an obfuscated Java payload disguised as decompiler.exe' performing environment checks and victim registration; Bitdefender confirms decompiler.exe is a JAR (MD5 d123dbb5...). Pairing the exact filename with xeno.exe/javaw parentage makes this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor • https://www.threatlocker.com/blog/powercat-malware-campaign-fake-game-cheats-deliver-infostealer-targeting-discord-roblox-and-crypto-wallets
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1027 T1082
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer running a legitimate Java decompiler tool that ships a launcher literally named decompiler.exe (rare, and normally not under AppData with a javaw parent)
  • Reverse-engineering workstation running JD-GUI/CFR-style tooling from a project folder
  • Security analyst detonating this exact sample in a lab
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\", @"\Java\jdk") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent chain xeno.exe→javaw→decompiler.exe and hash the decompiler.exe/JAR against Bitdefender IOCs; inspect its outbound connections for solthere.net /justacoolkat10 registration. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate the full javaw/decompiler tree, block solthere.net at proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts with decompiler.exe or GameDVR JAR persistence and reset all stealer-targeted account credentials (Roblox/Discord/Microsoft/crypto).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "decompiler.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("xeno.exe","javaw.exe","java.exe") or FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\decompiler.exe"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("xeno.exe","javaw.exe","java.exe") or NewProcessName has @"\AppData\Local\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Single process reading credential stores across 3+ browsers (stealer sweep) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the infostealer's browser-harvest stage: one non-browser process touching Login Data / Cookies / Web Data / Local State across three or more of Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera and Vivaldi in a short window. This fan-out across multiple browser families by a single process is the article's browser-data theft behaviour and is anomalous for legitimate software. Rationale: Encodes the article's explicit browser target list (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, Vivaldi) and the canonical Chromium credential files. The >=3-distinct-browser-families-by-one-process threshold is what separates the stealer's sweep from normal single-browser activity; this is a correlation/threshold detection so Sigma is intentionally omitted. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor • https://www.threatlocker.com/blog/powercat-malware-campaign-fake-game-cheats-deliver-infostealer-targeting-discord-roblox-and-crypto-wallets
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint backup/sync agents (OneDrive, corporate DLP, Code42) enumerating browser profiles
  • Password-manager importers pulling saved logins from multiple browsers at once
  • Browser-migration tools during onboarding
  • AV/EDR file-integrity scans reading Local State across browsers (usually a system/AV process — exclude by signer)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("onedrive.exe","code42service.exe","filecoauth.exe","mssense.exe","msmpeng.exe") and not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcess — javaw.exe/decompiler.exe/xeno.exe or any unsigned AppData binary = confirmed; signed backup/password-manager = likely FP. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the process, and force cookie/session revocation + password resets for the user's Google/Microsoft/gaming/crypto accounts (cookies enable MFA-bypass session theft). 3) Hunt: check the same process for Discord (%APPDATA%\discord\Local Storage), Roblox and Exodus wallet access, and correlate with solthere.net egress.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","Local State")
| extend Browser = case(
    FolderPath has @"\Google\Chrome\", "Chrome",
    FolderPath has @"\Microsoft\Edge\", "Edge",
    FolderPath has @"\BraveSoftware\", "Brave",
    FolderPath has @"\Opera Software\", "Opera",
    FolderPath has @"\Vivaldi\", "Vivaldi",
    "Other")
| where Browser != "Other"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","msedgewebview2.exe","explorer.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize BrowserFamilies = make_set(Browser), BrowserCount = dcount(Browser), FilesTouched = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| where BrowserCount >= 3   // 3+ distinct browser credential stores by one non-browser process = stealer sweep
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","Local State")
| extend Browser = case(
    TargetFilePath has @"\Google\Chrome\", "Chrome",
    TargetFilePath has @"\Microsoft\Edge\", "Edge",
    TargetFilePath has @"\BraveSoftware\", "Brave",
    TargetFilePath has @"\Opera Software\", "Opera",
    TargetFilePath has @"\Vivaldi\", "Vivaldi",
    "Other")
| where Browser != "Other"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","msedgewebview2.exe","explorer.exe"))
| summarize BrowserFamilies = make_set(Browser), BrowserCount = dcount(Browser), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessId, ActingProcessName
| where BrowserCount >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\Login Data OR *\Cookies OR *\Web Data OR *\Local State) @TargetFilename:(*\Google\Chrome\* OR *\Microsoft\Edge\* OR *\BraveSoftware\* OR *\Opera Software\* OR *\Vivaldi\*) -@Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\brave.exe OR *\opera.exe OR *\vivaldi.exe OR *\msedgewebview2.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo TargetFileName=/\\(Login Data|Cookies|Web Data|Local State)$/i
| regex("(?i)\\\\(Google\\\\Chrome|Microsoft\\\\Edge|BraveSoftware|Opera Software|Vivaldi)\\\\", field=TargetFileName)
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|brave|opera|vivaldi|msedgewebview2)\.exe$/i
| case { regex("(?i)Google\\\\Chrome", field=TargetFileName) | browser:="Chrome"; regex("(?i)Microsoft\\\\Edge", field=TargetFileName) | browser:="Edge"; regex("(?i)BraveSoftware", field=TargetFileName) | browser:="Brave"; regex("(?i)Opera Software", field=TargetFileName) | browser:="Opera"; regex("(?i)Vivaldi", field=TargetFileName) | browser:="Vivaldi"; * }
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId], function=count(field=browser, distinct=true, as=browser_count))
| browser_count >= 3
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name IN ("Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","Local State") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_id Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | eval browser=case(match(file_path,"(?i)\\\\Google\\\\Chrome\\\\"),"Chrome",match(file_path,"(?i)\\\\Microsoft\\\\Edge\\\\"),"Edge",match(file_path,"(?i)BraveSoftware"),"Brave",match(file_path,"(?i)Opera Software"),"Opera",match(file_path,"(?i)\\\\Vivaldi\\\\"),"Vivaldi") | where isnotnull(browser) | search NOT process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","msedgewebview2.exe") | stats dc(browser) as browser_count values(browser) as browsers values(file_path) as paths by dest process_name process_id | where browser_count>=3
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name IN ("Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","Local State") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_id Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | eval browser=case(match(file_path,"(?i)\\\\Google\\\\Chrome\\\\"),"Chrome",match(file_path,"(?i)\\\\Microsoft\\\\Edge\\\\"),"Edge",match(file_path,"(?i)BraveSoftware"),"Brave",match(file_path,"(?i)Opera Software"),"Opera",match(file_path,"(?i)\\\\Vivaldi\\\\"),"Vivaldi") | where isnotnull(browser) | search NOT process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","msedgewebview2.exe") | stats dc(browser) as browser_count values(browser) as browsers values(file_path) as paths by dest process_name process_id | where browser_count>=3
Exodus wallet app.asar tamper / SquirrelInteractive.bin drop by non-Exodus process AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the campaign's dedicated crypto-theft module: it tampers with the Exodus desktop wallet by injecting JavaScript into its app.asar and logs runtime wallet data to SquirrelInteractive.bin. A write to Exodus app.asar or the creation of SquirrelInteractive.bin by any process other than Exodus itself is an extremely high-fidelity wallet-compromise signal. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit Exodus Wallet callout plus Bitdefender's confirmed TTP: JS injection into Exodus app.asar and runtime logging to SquirrelInteractive.bin. app.asar is normally only written by the Exodus updater, so a foreign writer or the literal SquirrelInteractive.bin filename is a near-unique IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor
ATT&CKT1005 T1119 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Exodus auto-update writing app.asar (excluded via Exodus.exe/Update.exe parent)
  • A user manually reinstalling/repairing Exodus via msiexec
  • An Electron-app developer repacking app.asar with asar CLI on a dev box
  • AV quarantine renaming app.asar during remediation
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\exodus\" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("asar.exe","node.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "asar")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process is not Exodus/Update.exe; if it's javaw.exe/decompiler.exe/unsigned AppData binary, treat wallet as compromised. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the process, and instruct the user to move funds to a new wallet/seed from a clean device immediately — assume seed/keys exfiltrated. 3) Hunt: check for enumeration of other wallet dirs (Electrum, Ledger Live) under %APPDATA%\Roaming, and correlate SquirrelInteractive.bin creation time with solthere.net exfil connections.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "app.asar" and FolderPath has @"\exodus\") or FileName =~ "SquirrelInteractive.bin"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Exodus.exe","Update.exe","msiexec.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFileName =~ "app.asar" and TargetFilePath has @"\exodus\") or TargetFileName =~ "SquirrelInteractive.bin"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("Exodus.exe","Update.exe","msiexec.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

'Display Calibration' Run key persistence pointing to AppData javaw/GameDVR AIInstallation High
Hunts the campaign's persistence: a HKCU ...\CurrentVersion\Run value named 'Display Calibration' whose data launches the AppData JRE (javaw.exe) or the third-stage JAR staged in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\GameDVR. The benign-sounding value name paired with an AppData Java target is the specific autostart this malware writes. Rationale: Bitdefender confirms the Run value 'Display Calibration' and third-stage storage in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\GameDVR launched via the AppData javaw.exe. The specific value name plus AppData-Java target data is a distinctive autostart absent from clean systems (the real dccw.exe display-calibration tool never writes a Run key). Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate app coincidentally creating a Run entry named 'Display Calibration' (none known — Windows color calibration uses dccw.exe/scheduled task, not a Run key)
  • A benign Java desktop app legitimately installed under AppData\Local\Java setting autostart
  • Admin/GPO deploying a startup entry that references a GameDVR path
  • Manual analyst-created persistence in a test lab
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\") and RegistryValueData has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the RegistryValueData target and hash it against Bitdefender's GameDVR JAR IOC (163c8d11...); confirm the value is under HKCU Run. 2) Contain: isolate host, delete the 'Display Calibration' Run value and the StartupApproved\Run entry, kill the running javaw process, and remove the GameDVR-staged JAR. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same Run value name and GameDVR JAR, then reset all stealer-targeted credentials for affected users.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "Display Calibration"
   or RegistryValueData has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Java\jre\bin\javaw.exe", @"\Microsoft\GameDVR\", "decompiler")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dccw.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValue =~ "Display Calibration"
   or RegistryValueData has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Java\jre\bin\javaw.exe", @"\Microsoft\GameDVR\", "decompiler")
| where ActingProcessName !has "dccw.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Display Calibration Run Key Persistence to AppData Java Payload
id: 8a3f2c19-6d47-4e91-b0a5-1c9e7d4b2f60
description: Detects a CurrentVersion\Run value named 'Display Calibration' or Run data pointing to AppData\Local\Java javaw.exe / Microsoft\GameDVR, matching the fake Xeno/Powercat persistence.

#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate RegObjectName=/\\CurrentVersion\\Run$/i

Xeno RAT C2 egress to solthere.net / dynamic .xyz WebSocket from AppData Java AICommand & Control High
Hunts the RAT's command-and-control: victim registration and payload retrieval over solthere.net (/justacoolkat10, /api/v1/redeem) and a dynamically-generated .xyz WebSocket C2, driven by the AppData-resident javaw/decompiler process. Combines the hard domain IOC with the behavioural shape (Java from AppData reaching a fresh .xyz host) so it survives C2 rotation. Rationale: solthere.net (/justacoolkat10, /api/v1/redeem) is the confirmed registration+payload C2 from Bitdefender's IOC bundle for this exact campaign; the article notes the RAT generates its C2 URI dynamically, so the behavioural clause (AppData Java process reaching a .xyz host) backstops the domain IOC after rotation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor • https://hackread.com/microsoft-fake-xeno-roblox-utilities-windows-rat/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign Java desktop app under AppData legitimately contacting a .xyz SaaS/CDN endpoint (rare; tune the .xyz clause per environment)
  • Security researcher/sandbox resolving solthere.net for analysis
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling querying the domain
  • A user coincidentally visiting an unrelated .xyz site while a separate AppData Java app is active (mitigated by requiring same-process)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\") and RemoteUrl endswith ".xyz")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — javaw.exe/decompiler.exe from AppData confirms C2; capture the full URL path (/justacoolkat10, /api/v1/redeem). 2) Contain: block solthere.net and the observed .xyz host at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate the host, kill the Java process tree. 3) Hunt: pivot on the resolved IP for other victims, review DeviceNetworkEvents for the 500ms desktop-streaming/WebSocket beacon pattern, and reset all stealer-targeted credentials for the user.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "solthere.net"
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("javaw.exe","java.exe","decompiler.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\" and RemoteUrl endswith ".xyz")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "solthere.net" or DstHostname has "solthere.net" or (DstHostname endswith ".xyz" and Url has "solthere.net")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600

status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

18 Malicious npm Packages Deliver Cross-Platform RAT to Alibaba Tool Users

The Hacker News
2026-08-03 15 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have discovered a new set of malicious npm packages that target users of Alibaba developer tools with a cross-platform remote access trojan (RAT) as part of a sophisticated, targeted software supply chain attack targeting Chinese-speaking environments. One of the packages in question is "lib-mtop," an unscoped package with the same name as a private Alibaba package

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious @ali-impersonating npm packages installed into node_modules (Alibaba RAT cluster) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm/node loader spawning curl to fetch remote JavaScript from decoy Alibaba domains · [LLM] Linux RAT payload dropped to /tmp then self-deleted after in-memory load · [LLM] macOS RAT persistence via ~/.zshrc injection and 10-minute LaunchAgent · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network callback to decoy Alibaba OSS / Aliyun Function Compute RAT C2 hosts · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] mrmustard PyPI stealer exfil to metrics.femboy.energy / webhook.site · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Malicious @ali-impersonating npm packages installed into node_modules (Alibaba RAT cluster) AIDelivery High
Detects installation of the 18 named npm packages from the Socket-reported cross-platform RAT campaign that impersonate private @ali-scoped Alibaba packages. Fires on file writes into node_modules for any of the exact malicious package names, which is the earliest on-host signal of dependency-tree compromise. Rationale: Uses the complete verbatim package list from the article/Socket disclosure scoped to node_modules paths, so any hit is one of the exact malicious artifacts, not a generic supply-chain heuristic. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/npm-rat-targets-alibaba • https://cybersecuritynews.com/npm-packages-cross-platform-rat/ • https://gbhackers.com/split-rat-components-across-npm/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately named an internal package identically (e.g. a real private local-config-parser mirrored offline)
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating the packages in a sandbox
  • Package cache/mirror sync (Verdaccio/Nexus) replicating the names before removal
  • Old lockfile restore pulling a pre-March 2026 benign lib-mtop version
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","npm","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm which package + version installed and whether the host has access to the real @ali-scoped registry (the campaign only fully activates in Alibaba-adjacent environments). Check the package.json dependency tree for smart-config-manager as the bridge. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the developer host, kill node processes, remove node_modules, and treat the machine as compromised. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to UC2/UC3 on the same DeviceName for curl-fetched JS and the decoy aliyuncs/fcapp C2 callbacks; rotate any credentials, SSH keys, and cloud tokens present on the host from a clean machine.
DeviceFileEvents

| where FolderPath has "node_modules"
| where FolderPath has_any ("lib-mtop","aone-kit","aone-kit-cli","aone-sandbox","local-config-parser","smart-config-manager","cloud-config-fetcher","fast-transform-pipeline","aone-cloud-cli","colder-cli","def-open-client","feedback-ai-sdk","flight-compare-analyzer","lwp-web-client","lzd-unified-station-sdk","open-worker-cli","test-skill-zip","uniapi-bridge")

npm/node loader spawning curl to fetch remote JavaScript from decoy Alibaba domains AIInstallation High
Detects the lib-mtop loader behaviour where a Node/npm process shells out to curl to download a hardcoded remote JavaScript payload that is then executed via require(). Scopes to curl children of node/npm whose command line references the campaign's aliyuncs/fcapp/ai-app.pub decoy hosts. Rationale: Pairs the article's stated loader mechanic (node -> curl -> require) with the specific C2 host substrings, giving a parent-child + command-line triple that no legitimate npm workflow produces. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/npm-rat-targets-alibaba • https://cybersecuritynews.com/npm-packages-cross-platform-rat/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A build script legitimately using curl to pull a tarball from a real aliyuncs.com OSS bucket (verify exact subdomain against IOC list)
  • Node-based CI tooling that fetches assets via curl during install
  • Developer manually testing curl from an npm run-script
  • Internal package that vendors curl-based postinstall fetch of internal artifacts
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("registry.npmjs.org","github.com","githubusercontent.com"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Extract the full curl URL from the command line and compare the host against the IOC set (aone-cli-next.oss-cn-beijing.aliyuncs.com and siblings); benign OSS buckets differ in subdomain. Step 2 (contain): Kill the node and curl processes, block the resolved host at the proxy/firewall, isolate the host. Step 3 (hunt): Look for the downloaded JS being require()'d, any vm-module secondary payload, and follow-on OS-specific persistence (UC4/UC5) on the same DeviceName.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe","curl")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","npm","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("aliyuncs.com","fcapp.run","ai-app.pub")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "curl"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","pnpm","yarn")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("aliyuncs.com","fcapp.run","ai-app.pub")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network callback to decoy Alibaba OSS / Aliyun Function Compute RAT C2 hosts AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS/network egress to the campaign's payload-staging and C2 domains that masquerade as Alibaba OSS and Aliyun Function Compute endpoints to blend into legitimate Alibaba traffic. These full hostnames are hard IOCs from the article's pre-extracted set. Rationale: These are fully-qualified IOC hostnames unique to the campaign; the aone-* aliyuncs subdomains are attacker-controlled buckets distinct from generic *.aliyuncs.com, so exact-match keeps FP near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/npm-rat-targets-alibaba • https://gbhackers.com/split-rat-components-across-npm/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel sandbox or IOC-validation tooling resolving the hosts on purpose
  • Proxy/DNS security appliance pre-resolving submitted URLs for categorization
  • An analyst manually curling the IOC during investigation
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process (node/curl vs browser) and whether the resolution succeeded and returned data. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole/block the domains org-wide, isolate the resolving host, and snapshot for forensics. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with UC1/UC2 on the same host, review outbound bytes to the resolved IP for secondary-payload download, and sweep all dev hosts' DNS logs for the same five hosts.

Linux RAT payload dropped to /tmp then self-deleted after in-memory load AIInstallation Medium
Detects the Linux branch of the RAT that downloads a binary to /tmp, runs it as a detached process, and deletes the file from disk once loaded into memory. Correlates a short-lived /tmp file create+delete pair on the same host driven by a download/interpreter process. Rationale: Encodes the article's exact Linux TTP (download to /tmp, detached exec, delete-after-load) as a create+delete correlation restricted to download/interpreter processes, which is the defining anti-forensic behaviour of this branch. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/npm-rat-targets-alibaba
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Package managers extracting to /tmp and cleaning up (apt, pip build temp dirs)
  • Shell scripts using mktemp for transient work files
  • Compilers/CI writing and removing intermediate objects in /tmp
  • Browser or updater temp-download-then-move operations
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("mktemp","apt","dpkg","pip"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Recover the initiating command line and the /tmp filename; check whether the detached process is still resident (ps/lsof by inode) despite the on-disk file being gone. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, capture memory of the orphaned/detached process before reboot, and block associated C2. Step 3 (hunt): Tie back to UC1/UC3 for the npm install and aliyuncs download that seeded it, and check for lateral-movement attempts described as a final-payload capability.
let Created = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath startswith "/tmp/"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","wget","node","bash","sh")
| project CreateTime=Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileDeleted"
| where FolderPath startswith "/tmp/"
| project DeleteTime=Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath
| join kind=inner Created on DeviceName, FolderPath
| where DeleteTime between (CreateTime .. CreateTime + 5m)
| project DeviceName, FolderPath, CreateTime, DeleteTime, SecondsAlive=datetime_diff('second', DeleteTime, CreateTime), InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by CreateTime desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

macOS RAT persistence via ~/.zshrc injection and 10-minute LaunchAgent AIInstallation Medium
Detects the macOS branch of the RAT that persists by inserting a background script into ~/.zshrc and installing a LaunchAgent plist. Scopes file writes to those two persistence locations when driven by node/npm/curl/osascript rather than an interactive shell editor. Rationale: Combines the two named macOS persistence locations from the article with a non-interactive writer constraint (node/npm/curl/osascript), which cleanly separates the malware's scripted write from a developer editing their own shell profile. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/npm-rat-targets-alibaba
ATT&CKT1546.004 T1543.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dotfile managers (chezmoi, yadm) or Homebrew post-install writing to .zshrc
  • Legitimate app installers dropping their own LaunchAgent plist
  • Developer tooling (nvm, pyenv) appending shell-init lines to .zshrc
  • IDE/setup scripts registering a LaunchAgent for background services
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("chezmoi","yadm","brew","nvm","pyenv"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Read the injected .zshrc line / LaunchAgent plist ProgramArguments and check the referenced binary or URL against the campaign IOCs (aliyuncs/fcapp hosts). Note the LaunchAgent's 10-minute StartInterval as a strong tell. Step 2 (contain): Remove the persistence entries, unload the LaunchAgent, isolate the host, kill resident RAT processes. Step 3 (hunt): Check for injection into DingTalk/Wukong/Qoder collaboration apps, correlate to UC1's npm install, and rotate developer credentials from a clean machine.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName == ".zshrc" or FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","curl","osascript")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName == ".zshrc" or TargetFilePath contains "/Library/LaunchAgents/"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","curl","osascript")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

mrmustard PyPI stealer exfil to metrics.femboy.energy / webhook.site AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the secondary campaign in the article: the trojanized mrmustard 0.7.4 PyPI package whose _check_tf_compatibility() stealer harvests SSH keys, AWS creds and Kubernetes configs and beacons to metrics.femboy.energy/v1/collect (XOR key tf_compat_v2), with CI publishing-secret exfil to a webhook.site URL. Fires on egress to those hosts. Rationale: metrics.femboy.energy/v1/collect is the confirmed C2 (StepSecurity/SafeDep, decoded from XOR key tf_compat_v2) and the webhook.site GUID is the exact CI-secret exfil sink named in the article; both are hard IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-pypi-mrmustard-0-7-4-credential-stealer • https://safedep.io/mrmustard-malicious-pypi-package/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately using webhook.site for their own webhook testing (validate the exact GUID path)
  • Security research/detonation of mrmustard in a sandbox
  • IOC-validation curling the C2
  • webhook.site used by an unrelated internal integration test
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process (python importing mrmustard is the tell) and whether the destination is the exact webhook.site GUID vs generic testing. Confirm mrmustard 0.7.4 is installed (pip show). Step 2 (contain): Block femboy.energy and the webhook.site URL, isolate the host, and immediately treat SSH keys, AWS credentials, Kubernetes configs, and any CI publishing tokens on that host as compromised — rotate from a clean machine. Step 3 (hunt): Remove the three persistence mechanisms that survive uninstall, downgrade mrmustard, and audit CI runners for the self-hosted-runner probing / secret theft described in the report.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("metrics.femboy.energy","webhook.site/710babde-6ace-47fe-83f4-9688e6548df9")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "femboy.energy" or DnsQuery == "webhook.site"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
