``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)

SecurityEvent

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] N-central CVE-2026-18577 exploitation: inbound access from known attacker IPs
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rogue 'Cloudflared' Windows service registered post-N-central compromise · [LLM] Masqueraded svchost.exe running from a user's Documents folder · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] N-central C2: Cloudflared tunnel egress & Synology QuickConnect dynamic-DNS beacons · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
N-central CVE-2026-18577 exploitation: inbound access from known attacker IPs AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound network/web access to internet-facing N-able N-central RMM servers from the six IP addresses N-able published as active-exploitation indicators for the CVE-2026-18577 auth-bypass. Article-specific because it pins the exact IOC IP set tied to the admin-account-takeover campaign against N-central before build 2026.3.1.7. Rationale: Uses the exact six IOC IPs from N-able's hotfix-page advisory for CVE-2026-18577. Corroborated by Huntress and N-able status page; note Huntress found four of the initial IPs to be Mullvad/NordVPN exit nodes, so IP-only matching carries VPN-noise FP risk — treat as a pivot on the N-central host, not standalone conviction. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/n-able-vulnerability-exploitation • https://status.n-able.com/2026/08/02/n-central-2026-3-hotfix-1-mitigation-for-cve-2026-18577/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/08/03/cve-2026-18577-n-able-n-central-vulnerability/ • https://www.securityweek.com/n-able-patches-vulnerability-exploited-to-hack-n-central-servers/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin or MSP technician legitimately connecting to the N-central console through a Mullvad/NordVPN exit node that overlaps a published IOC IP
  • Security vendor / researcher scanning the N-central host from a shared VPN/hosting IP
  • Threat-intel enrichment or blocklist-validation tooling deliberately touching the IOC IPs
  • Shared cloud/CDN egress reusing an IP previously flagged in the campaign
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the matching host is an N-central server (or managed endpoint) and check its build — anything before 2026.3.1.7 is vulnerable. Pull the W3CIISLog rows for the IOC IP and inspect csUriStem/csUriQuery for admin/login route access without a preceding valid auth. 2) Contain: if the host is unpatched N-central, apply hotfix 2026.3.1.7 immediately, force-rotate all N-central admin credentials and API tokens, and block the IOC IPs at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3/UC4 on the same and downstream managed devices — look for a 'Cloudflared' service, svchost.exe in Documents, and tunnel egress; engage N-able support per advisory.
let iocIPs = dynamic(["173.249.252.200","87.249.138.34","37.19.210.32","68.235.46.214","37.153.90.88","92.118.112.181"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (iocIPs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let iocIPs = dynamic(["173.249.252.200","87.249.138.34","37.19.210.32","68.235.46.214","37.153.90.88","92.118.112.181"]);
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where cIP in (iocIPs)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUsername, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rogue 'Cloudflared' Windows service registered post-N-central compromise AIInstallation High
Detects registration of a Windows service named 'Cloudflared' (or a cloudflared binary installed as a service) — the exact persistence IOC N-able published for the CVE-2026-18577 campaign, where attackers stood up a Cloudflare tunnel service on compromised RMM-managed hosts. High-fidelity because a Cloudflared service is virtually never legitimate on an MSP-managed fleet. Rationale: The service name 'Cloudflared' is a verbatim IOC from N-able's hotfix download page, confirmed by Huntress ('registered a new service for a Cloudflare tunnel, enabling persistence'). A named Cloudflared service on managed endpoints is a near-zero-legitimacy signal in an MSP fleet. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/n-able-vulnerability-exploitation • https://status.n-able.com/2026/08/02/n-central-2026-3-hotfix-1-mitigation-for-cve-2026-18577/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/n-able-says-attackers-take-over-n.html
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An IT team that legitimately deploys Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) as a sanctioned remote-access solution across managed hosts
  • MSP-approved zero-trust tunneling pilot using cloudflared service install
  • Developer test box running cloudflared for local web-app exposure
  • Re-install/upgrade of an existing sanctioned cloudflared service generating a fresh 7045
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether Cloudflare Tunnel is a sanctioned tool in this environment; if not, treat as malicious. Capture the service ImagePath/binary hash and the InstalledBy account, and correlate the install time with N-central admin activity or the UC1 IOC IPs. 2) Contain: stop and disable the Cloudflared service, quarantine the binary, isolate the host, and revoke any Cloudflare tunnel token found in the service config or command line. 3) Hunt: sweep the whole managed fleet for the same service name and for svchost.exe in Documents (UC3) and tunnel egress to synology.me/quickconnect.to (UC4); rotate N-central admin creds.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ServiceInstalled"
| where AdditionalFields has "cloudflared" or FileName has "cloudflared" or FolderPath has "cloudflared"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (7045, 4697)
| where ServiceName =~ "Cloudflared" or ServiceFileName has "cloudflared"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, InstalledBy=SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceStartType, ServiceType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Masqueraded svchost.exe running from a user's Documents folder AIInstallation High
Detects execution of svchost.exe from outside System32/SysWOW64 — specifically inside a user Documents/profile path — the masquerading IOC N-able flagged for CVE-2026-18577. A genuine svchost.exe only ever runs from Windows\System32 (or SysWOW64), so any Documents-folder svchost.exe is a name-masquerade drop. Rationale: 'svchost.exe in the users' documents folder' is a direct quote from N-able's IOC list and re-stated by Help Net Security/Huntress ('review the Documents folder ... for a file called svchost.exe'). System-binary name + non-system path is a textbook masquerade with essentially no legitimate occurrence. Cross-checked against: • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/08/03/cve-2026-18577-n-able-n-central-vulnerability/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/n-able-vulnerability-exploitation • https://status.n-able.com/2026/08/02/n-central-2026-3-hotfix-1-mitigation-for-cve-2026-18577/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A backup/sync tool copying a real svchost.exe into a user Documents folder (rare, benign-file-move rather than execution)
  • Malware-analysis or IR sandbox intentionally running a copied svchost.exe from a working directory under Users
  • Software-packaging staging directory under a profile path that transiently holds a renamed system binary
  • Portable-app framework that bundles a helper named svchost.exe
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the svchost.exe in the Documents/profile path and compare against the legitimate Microsoft svchost.exe; check digital signature and parent process. Any unsigned/non-Microsoft binary here is malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the binary, kill the process, and capture memory for the running instance before removal. 3) Hunt: pivot on the parent process and InstalledBy account to find how it was dropped (likely via N-central Take Control), sweep the fleet for the same file/hash, and check for the Cloudflared service (UC2) and tunnel egress (UC4) on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| where FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows\\System32" and FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows\\SysWOW64" and FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows\\WinSxS"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Documents\", @"\Users\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\svchost.exe"
| where not(NewProcessName startswith "C:\\Windows\\System32" or NewProcessName startswith "C:\\Windows\\SysWOW64" or NewProcessName startswith "C:\\Windows\\WinSxS")
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\Documents\", @"\Users\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Masqueraded svchost.exe in Documents (N-central CVE-2026-18577)
id: c1a6f4d2-72b8-4e19-9a30-6f5b8e2c7d40

N-central C2: Cloudflared tunnel egress & Synology QuickConnect dynamic-DNS beacons AICommand & Control Medium
Detects command-and-control for the CVE-2026-18577 campaign: cloudflared-process outbound tunnels, connections to the six published IOC IPs, and DNS resolutions to the attacker's Synology QuickConnect / synology.me dynamic-DNS hosts. Article-specific via the exact C2 domains and the cloudflared abuse pattern N-able and Huntress described. Rationale: Combines the three verbatim C2 domains (mousears.synology.me, wagoosh/who-ripped-one.direct.quickconnect.to) with the six IOC IPs and the cloudflared abuse behaviour N-able/Huntress documented. A production N-central server subnet has no legitimate reason to tunnel via cloudflared or beacon to Synology QuickConnect dynamic-DNS. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/n-able-vulnerability-exploitation • https://status.n-able.com/2026/08/02/n-central-2026-3-hotfix-1-mitigation-for-cve-2026-18577/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/n-able-says-attackers-take-over-n.html
ATT&CKT1572 T1219 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user with a personal Synology NAS legitimately reaching *.quickconnect.to / *.synology.me from a workstation (not a server)
  • Sanctioned Cloudflare Tunnel deployment generating cloudflared egress
  • IT staff VPN'd through Mullvad/NordVPN overlapping an IOC IP
  • Backup/replication to a Synology appliance over QuickConnect from an authorized host
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("WKS", "LAPTOP", "DESKTOP") and RemoteUrl has_any ("synology.me", "quickconnect.to") and InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "cloudflared.exe" and RemoteIP !in ("173.249.252.200","87.249.138.34","37.19.210.32","68.235.46.214","37.153.90.88","92.118.112.181"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host and whether it's a server/RMM host (should never tunnel) vs a user workstation with a known personal NAS. Confirm the resolving process — cloudflared.exe or the masqueraded svchost.exe elevates confidence. 2) Contain: block the three C2 domains and six IOC IPs at DNS/egress, isolate the host, and terminate/disable any cloudflared tunnel and its token. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host resolving synology.me/quickconnect.to or connecting to the IOC IPs, correlate with the Cloudflared service (UC2) and Documents svchost.exe (UC3), and rotate all N-central admin and managed-endpoint credentials given god-mode RMM reach.
let c2Domains = dynamic(["mousears.synology.me","wagoosh.direct.quickconnect.to","who-ripped-one.direct.quickconnect.to"]);
let iocIPs = dynamic(["173.249.252.200","87.249.138.34","37.19.210.32","68.235.46.214","37.153.90.88","92.118.112.181"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cloudflared.exe"
    or RemoteIP in (iocIPs)
    or RemoteUrl in~ (c2Domains)
    or RemoteUrl has_any ("synology.me", "quickconnect.to")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2Domains = dynamic(["mousears.synology.me","wagoosh.direct.quickconnect.to","who-ripped-one.direct.quickconnect.to"]);
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery in~ (c2Domains) or DnsQuery has_any ("synology.me", "quickconnect.to")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DvcHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Google Password Manager Attacks Could Let Malware Hijack Passkey-Protected Accounts

The Hacker News
2026-08-03 9 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Malware running as an ordinary user on a Windows machine can sign into a victim's passkey-protected accounts without a fingerprint, a PIN, or anything at all appearing on the victim's screen. Unit 42 detailed three attack paths against Chrome's Google Password Manager cloud authenticator, which it calls Pass-ta-key, Silver Pass-ta-key and Golden Pass-ta-key; the strongest targets the master key

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Command line referencing Chrome passkey_enclave_state or Sync Data LevelDB path
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Google Password Manager Attacks Could Let Malware Hijack Passkey-Protected Accou
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Non-Chrome process reading chrome.exe memory to steal passkey Security Domain Secret (Golden Pass-ta-key) · [LLM] Non-Chrome process tampering with Chrome passkey_enclave_state or Sync Data LevelDB
Non-Chrome process reading chrome.exe memory to steal passkey Security Domain Secret (Golden Pass-ta-key) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a non-browser process opening a read handle into chrome.exe address space to scrape the 32-byte Security Domain Secret (SDS) while it sits in plaintext during passkey re-enrollment. Unit 42's Golden Pass-ta-key path reads the SDS out of Chrome process memory to decrypt all synced passkey private keys, so any non-Chrome, non-AV process reading Chrome memory is high-signal. Rationale: Uses the exact Golden Pass-ta-key behaviour from the Unit 42 report (SDS read from chrome.exe process memory) via Defender's raw OpenProcessApiCall/ReadProcessMemoryApiCall telemetry and Sysmon EID 10, scoping TargetImage=chrome.exe and excluding Chrome's own processes and AV. Datadog/Falcon left blank because neither the provided Sysmon EID subset nor an FDR process-access simpleName cleanly expresses cross-process read handles. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/google-authenticators-hidden-passkey-architecture/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft Defender (MsMpEng.exe) scanning Chrome memory
  • Endpoint DLP / EDR agents inspecting browser processes
  • Task Manager or Process Explorer opened by an admin to inspect Chrome
  • Crash-reporting tools (crashpad_handler) reading Chrome on a hang
  • Browser performance/telemetry agents with legitimate read access
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","taskmgr.exe","procexp64.exe","procexp.exe","MpDefenderCoreService.exe","SenseIR.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Google\Chrome\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName/SHA256 and folder path of the reader; confirm it is not AV/DLP/crashpad and is not signed by Google. Check GrantedAccess mask for PROCESS_VM_READ and whether the process was newly written to disk. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending process, and force a Google account passkey/SDS re-enrollment and PIN change for the signed-in user (assume all synced passkeys are compromised). 3) Hunt: pivot on the reader's SHA256 across the fleet, check for prior file access to passkey_enclave_state / Sync Data LevelDB, and review the affected Google account for anomalous passkey assertions or new device enrollments.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("OpenProcessApiCall", "ReadProcessMemoryApiCall")
| where FileName =~ "chrome.exe"                       // target process being read = Chrome
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "chrome.exe"      // Chrome's own multi-process reads are legit
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Google\Chrome\"   // exclude crashpad_handler / updater
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","taskmgr.exe","procexp64.exe","procexp.exe","csrss.exe","wininit.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcess = FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 10   // ProcessAccess
| where EventData has "chrome.exe"                                // TargetImage
| where EventData has_any ("0x1010","0x1410","0x1438","0x143a","0x1fffff","0x0010")  // GrantedAccess incl PROCESS_VM_READ
| where EventData !has @"\Google\Chrome\"                        // exclude Chrome/updater as the source
| where EventData !has "MsMpEng.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Chrome Process Reads Chrome Memory (Passkey SDS Theft)
id: 8f3a1d2e-6b74-4c9a-9e21-5c0f7a2b1d44
description: Detects a non-browser process opening a read handle into chrome.exe to scrape the passkey Security Domain Secret (Unit 42 Golden Pass-ta-key)
references:

logsource:

detection:
  selection:
    TargetImage|endswith: '\chrome.exe'

      - '0x1010'
      - '0x1410'
      - '0x1438'

  filter_chrome:

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=chrome.exe) by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search parent_process_name!=chrome.exe AND parent_process!="*\\Google\\Chrome\\*" AND parent_process_name!="MsMpEng.exe" AND parent_process_name!="taskmgr.exe" | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Non-Chrome process tampering with Chrome passkey_enclave_state or Sync Data LevelDB AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a non-Chrome process writing, copying, renaming, or deleting Chrome's passkey device-key store (passkey_enclave_state) or the synced-credential LevelDB. Copy-out feeds offline SDS/passkey recovery; deletion forces the device re-enrollment window that Silver/Golden Pass-ta-key abuse to register an attacker UV key. Rationale: Anchored on the exact artifacts named in the Unit 42 report — passkey_enclave_state (wrapped device key + SDS + PIN) and the Sync Data\LevelDB WebauthnCredentialSpecifics store — with any non-Chrome, non-Google-signed writer/deleter surfaced. Deletion maps to the forced re-enrollment window abused by Silver/Golden; copy-out maps to offline recovery. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1556
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OneDrive / enterprise backup agents syncing the Chrome profile folder
  • Chrome profile migration or roaming-profile tooling
  • Antivirus quarantine touching files under User Data
  • Admin manually deleting a corrupt Chrome profile to fix sync
  • Endpoint management agents wiping browser data on offboarding
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe","MsMpEng.exe","MpDefenderCoreService.exe","backup.exe","cbsystray.exe") and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "Google LLC"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is not Google-signed, OneDrive, or backup software; note ActionType (Delete vs Create/Modify) and whether a copy of passkey_enclave_state / LevelDB landed outside the profile. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill/quarantine the process, and treat the user's synced passkeys as compromised — trigger passkey re-enrollment and PIN rotation on the Google account. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (chrome.exe memory reads) on the same host, search for exfil of the copied store over the network, and review the Google account for new device enrollments or attacker-registered UV keys.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "passkey_enclave_state"
      or (FolderPath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\" and FolderPath has @"\Sync Data\LevelDB")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "chrome.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "Google LLC"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Google\Chrome\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe","backup.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "passkey_enclave_state"
      or (TargetFilePath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\" and TargetFilePath has @"\Sync Data\LevelDB")
| where ActingProcessName !has @"\chrome.exe"
| where ActingProcessName !has @"\Google\Chrome\"
| where ActingProcessName !has @"\OneDrive.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Chrome Access to Chrome Passkey Enclave State / Sync LevelDB
id: b21c7e4f-9a08-4d13-8b6e-2f7c1a9d5e30
description: Detects non-Chrome processes writing, renaming or deleting Chrome's passkey_enclave_state device-key store or the Sync Data LevelDB (Unit 42 Pass-ta-key family)
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/03
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1555.003
  - attack.t1556
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_name:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '\passkey_enclave_state'
  selection_leveldb:
    TargetFilename|contains|all:
      - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
      - '\Sync Data\LevelDB\'
  filter_chrome:
    Image|contains: '\Google\Chrome\'
  condition: (selection_name or selection_leveldb) and not filter_chrome
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\\passkey_enclave_state OR *\\PASSKEY_ENCLAVE_STATE) OR (@TargetFilename:*\\User?Data\\* AND @TargetFilename:*\\LevelDB\\*)) NOT @Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\CHROME.EXE) NOT @Image:*\\Google\\Chrome\\*
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| (TargetFileName=/\\passkey_enclave_state$/i OR TargetFileName=/\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\.*\\Sync Data\\LevelDB\\/i)
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\chrome\.exe$/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\Google\\Chrome\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name=passkey_enclave_state OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\*\\Sync Data\\LevelDB\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search process_name!=chrome.exe AND process_name!="*\\Google\\Chrome\\*" | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name=passkey_enclave_state OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\*\\Sync Data\\LevelDB\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search process_name!=chrome.exe AND process_name!="*\\Google\\Chrome\\*" | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Command line referencing Chrome passkey_enclave_state or Sync Data LevelDB path AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts LOLBins/scripts (cmd, powershell, esentutl, robocopy, xcopy) invoked with Chrome's passkey store path on the command line — the tooling-based variant of Pass-ta-key local reconnaissance that enumerates relying parties, usernames and encrypted passkey material. Rationale: Targets the article's stated local-recon step (reading credential IDs, relying parties and usernames from Sync Data\LevelDB) plus the passkey_enclave_state path from the Unit 42 report, catching the copy/enumeration variant that uses native tooling rather than in-process API reads. Lower confidence/hunting tier because sophisticated malware reads via API and leaves nothing on the command line. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html
ATT&CKT1217 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Support/IT scripts backing up or clearing a Chrome profile
  • Forensic/DFIR triage collection referencing the LevelDB path
  • Browser-data migration utilities
  • Developer debugging Chrome sync with the path in a script
  • Security tooling that inventories browser credential stores
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccmexec.exe","MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") and not (AccountName has_any ("svc-dfir","admin-backup"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the full command line and parent process — is this an admin/DFIR script, a migration tool, or an unexpected LOLBin (esentutl/robocopy/powershell) run by a standard user? Check the executing account and host role. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, isolate the host and kill the process; preserve any output/copy of the passkey store for IR and rotate the affected Google account passkeys. 3) Hunt: pivot on the parent process and user to UC1/UC2 (chrome memory reads and file tamper), check for archive/exfil of the collected data, and sweep the fleet for the same command-line pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("passkey_enclave_state", @"Sync Data\LevelDB")
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data" or ProcessCommandLine has "passkey_enclave_state"
| where FileName !~ "chrome.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "chrome.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("passkey_enclave_state", @"Sync Data\LevelDB")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "passkey_enclave_state"
| where TargetProcessName !has @"\chrome.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Command Line Referencing Chrome Passkey Store Path
id: c9d4f2a7-1e63-4b58-a0c2-7d9e5f81b3a6
description: Detects processes invoked with Chrome's passkey_enclave_state or Sync Data LevelDB path on the command line (Unit 42 Pass-ta-key local recon / copy-out)
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering

tags:
  - attack.discovery
  - attack.t1217

  - attack.t1555.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation

detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'passkey_enclave_state'
      - '\Sync Data\LevelDB'
  filter:
    Image|endswith: '\chrome.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:(*passkey_enclave_state* OR *PASSKEY_ENCLAVE_STATE* OR *Sync?Data\\LevelDB*) NOT @Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\CHROME.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| CommandLine=/passkey_enclave_state|Sync Data\\LevelDB/i
| NOT ImageFileName=/\\chrome\.exe$/i

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*passkey_enclave_state*" OR Processes.process="*Sync Data\\LevelDB*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search process_name!=chrome.exe | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*passkey_enclave_state*" OR Processes.process="*Sync Data\\LevelDB*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search process_name!=chrome.exe | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.

INC Ransomware Emerges as Dominant Actor Exploiting SonicWall SMA 1000 Flaws

The Hacker News
2026-08-03 15 use cases 4 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

The INC Ransomware operation has emerged as the "dominant threat actor" exploiting the recently disclosed security flaws in SonicWall Secure Mobile Access (SMA) 1000 series VPN appliances. In a report published over the weekend, Resecurity said it observed the INC Ransomware accelerating its activity since the beginning of August 2026, listing multiple victims on its data leak site. Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SonicWall SMA 1000 /wsproxy exploitation (CVE-2026-15409/15410) by UTA0533/INC · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound network/VPC callbacks to UTA0533/INC Ransomware C2 IPs · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] INC Ransomware encryption: INC-README note drop and .INC mass file rename · [LLM] INC extortion infrastructure contact: helprans.com email and DNS/web callbacks · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
SonicWall SMA 1000 /wsproxy exploitation (CVE-2026-15409/15410) by UTA0533/INC AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP(S) requests to the SonicWall SMA 1000 /wsproxy endpoint, the exact endpoint Volexity/Resecurity identified as the unauthenticated exploitation vector where spoofed client identifiers open a WebSocket tunnel to localhost-only CouchDB/ctrl-service. Surfaces external source IPs interacting with /wsproxy and flags any that match known attacker infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the exact /wsproxy endpoint named by Resecurity ('Identify external source addresses that interacted with /wsproxy') and corroborated by Volexity as the CVE-2026-15409/15410 exploit path; enriches with the 8 article IOC IPs as a KnownBadSource flag. Appliance-only, so Defender/Falcon/Datadog left empty (SMA is a Linux VPN box, not an EDR-covered endpoint). Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://www.resecurity.com/blog/article/from-wsproxy-to-root-inc-ransomware-and-sonicwall-sma-exploit-chain • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/sonicwall-sma1000-flaws-exploited-as-zero-days-to-push-custom-malware/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SMA 1000 WebSocket client sessions from internal user ranges
  • SonicWall management/health-check probes hitting /wsproxy
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) authorised to test the appliance
  • Load-balancer or reverse-proxy keepalive traffic to the endpoint
Suppression filter
| where KnownBadSource == "YES" or SourceIP !startswith "10." and SourceIP !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SourceIP list hitting /wsproxy; cross-check against the 8 IOC IPs and any external/geo-anomalous source; confirm whether appliance is on patched SMA 1000 firmware (mid-July 2026 fix). 2) Contain: if an external/IOC source is confirmed, block the source IP at the perimeter, isolate the SMA appliance, force firmware patch, and rotate ALL VPN credentials, session tokens and TOTP MFA seeds (Rapid7 confirmed these were harvested). 3) Hunt: review appliance for KNUCKLEBALL Python scripts in site-packages, Suo5/ORANGETAIL processes, and the ROOTRUN setuid ELF; pivot to internal hosts reachable via the appliance for lateral movement.
let C2IPs = dynamic(["108.205.8.173","147.45.51.19","150.241.210.53","202.8.105.201","217.77.15.99","42.200.172.14","81.19.140.217","89.117.20.1"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor has "SonicWall" or DeviceProduct has_any ("SMA","Secure Mobile Access")
| where RequestURL has "/wsproxy"
| summarize RequestCount = count(), Methods = make_set(RequestMethod, 10), UserAgents = make_set(RequestClientApplication, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DestinationIP
| extend KnownBadSource = iff(SourceIP in (C2IPs), "YES", "NO")
| order by KnownBadSource desc, RequestCount desc

Outbound network/VPC callbacks to UTA0533/INC Ransomware C2 IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any internal host or cloud workload connecting to the eight command-and-control IP addresses tied to the SonicWall SMA 1000 exploitation campaign (used by Suo5 reverse-proxy tunnels and INC operations). Pure IOC match against network telemetry across endpoint, firewall and VPC flow. Rationale: Exact eight IPs from the article's pre-extracted IOC set, corroborated across Volexity/BleepingComputer/Resecurity reporting on the same UTA0533/INC campaign; direct-IP match on network telemetry is inherently high-fidelity. VPC Flow variant included because Suo5 reverse-proxy callbacks also apply to AWS-hosted victims. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/inc-ransomware-emerges-as-dominant.html • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/07/17/proxying-to-compromise-sonicwall-secure-mobile-access-0-day-exploitation/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/sonicwall-sma1000-flaws-exploited-as-zero-days-to-push-custom-malware/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/sandbox VMs deliberately beaconing to the IOCs
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse where a benign service later occupies the same address
  • Security scanners validating blocklists against these IPs
  • IR responders actively probing the infrastructure
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal SourceIP/host and initiating process; confirm the connection is not from a sanctioned security tool. 2) Contain: block all eight IPs at perimeter and EDR, isolate the connecting host, and capture volatile memory before reimage. 3) Hunt: pivot from the host to check for Suo5 tunneling, INC ransom-note drops, credential theft, and other hosts touching the same IOC set; correlate connection timestamps with /wsproxy exploitation on the SMA appliance.

INC Ransomware encryption: INC-README note drop and .INC mass file rename AIActions on Objectives High
Detects INC Ransomware impact activity on internal Windows hosts following SMA 1000 compromise: creation of the corroborated ransom-note files (INC-README.txt/html, INC_README.txt) and/or mass renaming of files to the .INC encrypted extension by a single process. The note filenames alone are near-certain TPs. Rationale: INC ransom-note filenames (INC-README.txt/html, INC_README.txt) and the .INC extension are corroborated by SentinelOne's INC profile and Secureworks GOLD IONIC reporting; the article names INC as the dominant actor. Note-file creation is near-zero-FP; the .INC branch requires >20 files to separate mass encryption from benign include files. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/anthology/inc-ransom/ • https://www.secureworks.com/blog/gold-ionic-deploys-inc-ransomware • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/inc-ransomware-emerges-as-dominant.html
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer source trees containing legitimate .INC include files (ASP/PHP) being written en masse by a build/deploy
  • Backup or archival tooling copying pre-existing .INC files
  • A file named INC_README in benign software documentation
  • Bulk file operations by a migration script hitting the >20 threshold
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\inetpub\", @"\wwwroot\", @"\source\", @"\git\") and EncFiles > 0 and NoteFiles == 0)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the InitiatingProcess/SHA256 and whether a genuine INC-README note (not a .INC include file) was written; check the process parentage and origin host. 2) Contain: isolate the host from the network immediately, kill the encrypting process, and preserve the ransom note + a sample encrypted file for recovery/decryptor analysis; do NOT reboot. 3) Hunt: expand the InitiatingProcessSHA256 across all hosts, check for prior VSS deletion and lateral movement from the SMA appliance, and rotate credentials given confirmed harvesting on the SMA.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FileName in~ ("INC-README.txt","INC-README.html","INC_README.txt","INC_README.html") or FileName endswith ".INC"
| summarize NoteFiles = countif(FileName has "INC-README" or FileName has "INC_README"), EncFiles = countif(FileName endswith ".INC"), AffectedDirs = dcount(FolderPath), SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 15), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where NoteFiles > 0 or EncFiles > 20
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("INC-README.txt","INC-README.html","INC_README.txt","INC_README.html") or TargetFileExtension =~ "INC"
| summarize NoteFiles = countif(TargetFileName has "README"), EncFiles = countif(TargetFileExtension =~ "INC"), SampleFiles = make_set(TargetFileName, 15), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName
| where NoteFiles > 0 or EncFiles > 20
| order by LastSeen desc

INC extortion infrastructure contact: helprans.com email and DNS/web callbacks AIActions on Objectives High
Detects communication with helprans.com - the domain INC operators (caller 'Andrew', +1 304-384-0401, info@helprans.com) provided to victims for extortion negotiation. Covers inbound extortion email from the domain (Defender) and DNS/proxy resolution of the domain across the estate. Rationale: helprans.com and info@helprans.com are the article's unique extortion-contact IOCs (tied to caller 'Andrew' / +1 304-384-0401), corroborated by Resecurity; any email, DNS or proxy interaction with this domain is high-fidelity. Sentinel has no EmailEvents equivalent so its query covers DNS/proxy while Defender covers the email pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/inc-ransomware-emerges-as-dominant.html • https://www.resecurity.com/blog/article/from-wsproxy-to-root-inc-ransomware-and-sonicwall-sma-exploit-chain
ATT&CKT1657 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC analyst or mail-security sandbox resolving/opening the domain during triage
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment auto-resolving the indicator
  • A legitimately similarly-named but unrelated domain (verify exact FQDN match)
  • Quarantined extortion email being replayed by a security-testing tool
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the hit is inbound extortion email (confirms an active extortion attempt / prior compromise) or an outbound DNS/proxy callback; identify the affected recipient/host. 2) Contain: block helprans.com and info@helprans.com at mail gateway, DNS and proxy; quarantine the email and preserve it; if a host resolved the domain, isolate and investigate for INC encryption. 3) Hunt: treat any helprans.com contact as evidence of compromise - pivot to the SMA appliance for /wsproxy exploitation, the eight C2 IPs, and INC ransom-note activity across the estate.
let dom = "helprans.com";
union
(EmailEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SenderFromDomain =~ dom or SenderMailFromDomain =~ dom | extend Signal = "ExtortionEmail", Detail = strcat(SenderFromAddress, " -> ", RecipientEmailAddress, " | ", Subject), Host = tostring(RecipientEmailAddress)),
(DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RemoteUrl has dom | extend Signal = "NetworkCallback", Detail = strcat(InitiatingProcessFileName, " -> ", RemoteUrl), Host = DeviceName)
| project Timestamp, Signal, Host, Detail
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has "helprans.com" | project TimeGenerated, Signal = "DNS", Src = ClientIP, Detail = Name),
(CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationHostName has "helprans.com" or RequestURL has "helprans.com" | project TimeGenerated, Signal = "Proxy", Src = SourceIP, Detail = coalesce(RequestURL, DestinationHostName))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inside the Underground Business of the Android BTMOB RAT malware

BleepingComputer
2026-08-03 7 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Flare researchers analyzed thousands of underground posts to examine how the BTMOB Android malware operation evolved into a fragmented ecosystem of resellers, source-code vendors, custom versions, and competing sales channels. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] BTMOB RAT APK sample hash observed on managed endpoint · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Inside the Underground Business of the Android BTMOB RAT malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] BTMOB Android RAT C2 beacon to server.yaarsa.com / 78.135.93.123 · [LLM] BTMOB RAT C2 URI path /yaarsa/private/ and WebSocket /con endpoint
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
BTMOB Android RAT C2 beacon to server.yaarsa.com / 78.135.93.123 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network connections and DNS resolutions from any monitored endpoint (including Defender/Falcon mobile agents and corporate proxy/firewall) to the confirmed BTMOB RAT C2 infrastructure. High-fidelity because the IP and WebSocket C2 domain are corroborated by Palo Alto Unit42 and Cyble as dedicated BTMOB operator infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the confirmed C2 IP 78.135.93.123 and WebSocket C2 domain server.yaarsa.com; both appear in Palo Alto Unit42's BTMOB IOC list and Cyble's analysis (hxxp://78.135.93.123/yaarsa/private/ and hxxp://server.yaarsa.com/con), making them dedicated-infrastructure indicators rather than shared hosting. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/PaloAltoNetworks/Unit42-timely-threat-intel/blob/main/2025-05-21-IOCs-for-BTMOB-RAT-activity.txt • https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/ • https://any.run/malware-trends/btmob/
ATT&CKT1437.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware sandbox or MTD detonation lab intentionally resolving/connecting to server.yaarsa.com
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling proactively resolving the C2 domain from a SOC workstation
  • IP 78.135.93.123 later reassigned by the hosting provider to a benign tenant
  • Security crawler or blocklist-feed validator probing the domain
  • Analyst manually browsing the C2 URL during triage
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating device and process; if it is a corporate mobile/MDM-managed device, treat as likely compromised — confirm it is not a sandbox/scanner asset. 2) Contain: block 78.135.93.123 and server.yaarsa.com at proxy/firewall/DNS, isolate the device, and force credential resets for accounts used on that phone (BTMOB harvests logins via Accessibility overlays). 3) Hunt: pivot on the device for the BTMOB APK hashes (see companion UC), check for other endpoints resolving server.yaarsa.com or the extended Unit42 C2 IP set, and review authentication logs for logins sourced from the infected device post-infection.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "78.135.93.123" or RemoteUrl has "server.yaarsa.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
union
( CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationIP == "78.135.93.123" or DestinationHostName has "server.yaarsa.com" or RequestURL has "server.yaarsa.com"
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DeviceProduct, Activity ),
( DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Name has "server.yaarsa.com"
  | project TimeGenerated, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResolvedIP = Result )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BTMOB RAT C2 URI path /yaarsa/private/ and WebSocket /con endpoint AICommand & Control High
Hunts web-proxy/URL telemetry for the distinctive BTMOB C2 request patterns: the PHP handler path /yaarsa/private/ and the server.yaarsa.com/con WebSocket endpoint. Distinct from the IP/DNS pivot because it survives C2 IP rotation and catches the exact application-layer request shape documented by Cyble. Rationale: Uses Cyble's documented BTMOB C2 application-layer artefacts: the PHP handler path hxxp://78.135.93.123/yaarsa/private/yarsap_80541.php and the WebSocket endpoint hxxp://server.yaarsa.com/con carrying the 'BTMOB'/'BT-v' handshake — path strings that are unique to this RAT family. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because their standard telemetry (Sysmon EID3, FDR NetworkConnect, CloudTrail) does not carry full request URIs. Cross-checked against: • https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/ • https://any.run/malware-trends/btmob/
ATT&CKT1437.001 T1521
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Proxy content-inspection appliance replaying/sanitising the captured URL
  • Security web crawler or URL sandbox fetching the C2 path during analysis
  • Analyst manually retrieving the C2 URI while investigating a sample
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source host and whether the request succeeded (HTTP 101/200 to /con indicates an established WebSocket beacon = active compromise, not a one-off probe). 2) Contain: block server.yaarsa.com and the URI patterns at the proxy, isolate the source device, and revoke sessions/credentials entered on it. 3) Hunt: sweep proxy logs for any host hitting /yaarsa/private/ or */con on BTMOB C2 hosts, and correlate with the BTMOB APK-hash file detection to confirm the implant on the device.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/yaarsa/private/" or (RemoteUrl has "server.yaarsa.com" and RemoteUrl has "/con")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
union
( CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where RequestURL has "/yaarsa/private/" or RequestURL has "server.yaarsa.com/con"
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DeviceProduct, RequestClientApplication ),
( ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Url has "/yaarsa/private/" or Url has "server.yaarsa.com/con"
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname = HttpHostName, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
