| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("huggingface.co")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["huggingface.co"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-18577", "CVE-2026-18556")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-18577", "CVE-2026-18556")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Galaxy Research mapped the sweep and tied it to a firmware flaw in Coldcard, the Bitcoin-only hardware wallet made by Canadian firm Coinkite. Actions on Objectives

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Rails patches critical Active Storage flaw with RCE potential

BleepingComputer
2026-08-01 6 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

A critical vulnerability in the Active Storage framework can allow an unauthenticated attacker to read arbitrary files from a Rails application, and potentially escalate to remote code execution (RCE). [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Active Storage crafted image upload to libvips variant endpoints (CVE-2026-66066) · [LLM] Exposure hunt: hosts with vulnerable libvips / Rails Active Storage (CVE-2026-66066)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rails app worker spawning shell or network child (KindaRails2Shell RCE)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Rails/Ruby worker reading secret_key_base and credential files post-upload (CVE-2026-66066) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Active Storage crafted image upload to libvips variant endpoints (CVE-2026-66066) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts unauthenticated traffic to Rails Active Storage upload and variant/representation endpoints, the exploitation surface for CVE-2026-66066 (KindaRails2Shell) where a crafted image drives libvips into an arbitrary-file-read. Surfaces sources that both submit uploads and request server-side image processing so an analyst can triage the file-read primitive. Rationale: Uses the canonical Rails Active Storage route prefixes (/rails/active_storage/direct_uploads, /representations/, /blobs/, /disk/) — corroborated by Rapid7/Ethiack as the direct-upload + variant-processing surface. Technical PoC strings were withheld by the researchers, so this is a triage hunt on the exploit surface rather than a signature. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/kindarails2shell-rails-rce-cve-2026-66066 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-rails-flaw-could-let.html
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate users uploading avatars/profile pictures and viewing generated thumbnails
  • Load/synthetic monitoring hitting upload endpoints
  • CDN or image-proxy warming Active Storage representations in bulk
  • Mobile app clients using direct_uploads at high volume
  • Security scanners (internal ASM/DAST) probing the same routes
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(SrcIpAddr) and SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the raw requests for the top source IPs — check whether they are unauthenticated, whether upload requests are immediately followed by representation/variant requests, and whether responses are anomalously sized (leaked file content). 2) Contain: if libvips <8.13 or the app is unpatched (Rails <7.2.3.2/8.0.5.1/8.1.3.1), block the source at the WAF/reverse-proxy and enable VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host to UC 'Rails worker sensitive-file access' and 'Rails worker spawning shell/network child' to confirm file-read and RCE.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/rails/active_storage/"
| where Url has_any ("/representations/", "/blobs/", "/direct_uploads", "/disk/")
| summarize Requests = count(), Methods = make_set(HttpMethod, 10), Statuses = make_set(HttpStatusCode, 10), SampleUrls = make_set(Url, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Rails Active Storage libvips Variant Endpoint Access (CVE-2026-66066)
id: 5c9d7f2a-3e14-4b8a-9c21-8f0a6d1e4b77
description: Detects requests to Rails Active Storage upload/variant endpoints abused by CVE-2026-66066 (KindaRails2Shell) to trigger libvips arbitrary file read.
references:

  - https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/kindarails2shell-rails-rce-cve-2026-66066
  - https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/

Rails/Ruby worker reading secret_key_base and credential files post-upload (CVE-2026-66066) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the Rails application process (ruby/puma/unicorn/passenger) accessing sensitive secret and environment files — the credential-access step of CVE-2026-66066 where the libvips arbitrary-file-read is used to exfiltrate secret_key_base, master.key, credentials.yml.enc, .env and /proc/self/environ. High-fidelity because a running web worker should not be reading these at request time. Rationale: Ties the standard Rails secret paths named in the article (secret_key_base, master.key, database/cloud creds in the process environment) to the app-server process identity — a Rails worker reading /proc/self/environ or master.key at runtime is the direct fingerprint of the file-read primitive being abused. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-rails-flaw-could-let.html • https://socprime.com/blog/cve-2026-66066-critical-rails-flaw-exposes-server-files-via-image-uploads/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Normal app boot reading config/master.key and credentials.yml.enc during initialization (baseline once per deploy/restart)
  • dotenv gems loading .env at startup
  • Config-management/CI tooling templating credential files
  • APM/observability agents enumerating process environment
  • Developer console (rails c) sessions on a jump host
Suppression filter
| where ActionType != "FileCreated" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "rails console" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "assets:precompile"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the access is at request-serving time (not process boot) and correlate the host/timestamp with UC1 Active Storage upload traffic within the same window. 2) Contain: treat secret_key_base, DB and Active Storage credentials as compromised — rotate them, rotate the Rails master key, and patch to Rails 7.2.3.2/8.0.5.1/8.1.3.1 with libvips ≥8.13. 3) Hunt: search for forged session cookies / anomalous authenticated sessions and pivot to UC3 for shell/network children of the worker.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "bundle", "rails")
| where FileName in~ ("credentials.yml.enc", "master.key", "environ", ".env")
    or FolderPath has_any ("/config/credentials", "/proc/self/environ")
| where FolderPath !startswith "/tmp/" and FolderPath !has "/active_storage/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "bundle", "rails")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/config/credentials.yml.enc", "/config/master.key", "/config/credentials/", "/proc/self/environ")
    or TargetFileName =~ ".env"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessId, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rails app worker spawning shell or network child (KindaRails2Shell RCE) AIInstallation High
Detects the Rails/Ruby application server (puma/unicorn/passenger/ruby) spawning an unexpected shell or network client (sh, bash, curl, wget, nc, python, ruby -e) — the RCE execution stage where a forged, secret_key_base-signed serialized payload drives insecure deserialization into command execution on the host. Rationale: A web application worker (puma/unicorn/passenger/ruby) is not expected to fork shells or curl/wget at runtime; pairing that specific parent set with shell/network children is the highest-fidelity signal of the deserialization-to-RCE endgame the article and Akamai describe. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/kindarails2shell-rails-rce-cve-2026-66066
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rails app legitimately shelling out to ImageMagick/ffmpeg/git via system() for background jobs
  • Sidekiq/Resque workers running rake tasks that invoke curl/bash
  • Health-check or entrypoint scripts (bash) launched by the app container
  • Deploy hooks calling shell from within the app process
  • Ruby scripts using backticks for legitimate ops tooling
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert", "identify", "vipsthumbnail", "ffmpeg", "/rake", "sidekiq", "healthcheck"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line — reverse-shell one-liners, curl to unknown IPs, or writes to /tmp are strong TP indicators; benign image/rake tooling is FP. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the spawned process tree, and treat app secrets as compromised (rotate secret_key_base + all DB/cloud creds). 3) Hunt: pull outbound connections from the child, correlate back to the originating Active Storage upload (UC1) and credential-file reads (UC2), and search other Rails hosts for the same parent→child pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "rails", "bundle")
| where FileName in~ ("sh", "bash", "dash", "curl", "wget", "nc", "ncat", "python", "python3", "perl")
    or (FileName in~ ("ruby") and ProcessCommandLine has "-e ")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "rails", "bundle")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh", "/bash", "/dash", "/curl", "/wget", "/nc", "/ncat", "/python", "/perl")
    or (ActingProcessName has "/ruby" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "-e ")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposure hunt: hosts with vulnerable libvips / Rails Active Storage (CVE-2026-66066) AIExploitation High
Surfaces internet-facing hosts still exposed to CVE-2026-66066 — libvips before 8.13 (which cannot disable the unfuzzed operations at all) or unpatched Rails Active Storage. Drives pre-exploitation prioritization since public PoCs are already circulating. Rationale: Directly keys on the article's named CVE (CVE-2026-66066) and the libvips 8.13 fix floor; scoping to internet-facing hosts turns the vuln feed into an actionable, prioritized exposure list ahead of the disclosed public PoCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://www.linuxcompatible.org/story/rails-7232-8051-and-8131-active-storage-security-patch-targets-cve202666066
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts that use ImageMagick (not libvips) as the Active Storage processor — not actually exploitable
  • Apps that do not accept untrusted image uploads (internal-only) — lower real risk
  • TVM version-string mismatch flagging a backported/distro-patched libvips as vulnerable
  • Rails 6.x using Active Storage defaults (not affected) still flagged by generic version match
  • Decommissioned/quarantined hosts still in inventory
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each flagged host confirm it uses the vips processor and accepts untrusted uploads (else de-prioritize), and check internet exposure. 2) Contain: patch Active Storage to 7.2.3.2/8.0.5.1/8.1.3.1, upgrade libvips to ≥8.13, and set VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED / Vips.block_untrusted(true); apply WAF virtual patch where immediate upgrade isn't possible. 3) Hunt: retro-scan UC1/UC2/UC3 telemetry on every exposed host for prior exploitation before the patch window.

Adform detected the incident on July 27, 2026, removed the malicious code, notified affected clients, and reported it to authorities. Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Confirmed Adform supply-chain victim: poisoned script load + beacon to attacker IP · [LLM] Exposure scoping: hosts that loaded poisoned Adform trackpoint-async.js (Jul 26-28 2026) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hackers Poison Adform Script to Swap Crypto Wallet Addresses Across Customer Sit
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Adform crypto-swap stealer C2/exfil beacon to 84.32.102.230:7744 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Adform crypto-swap stealer C2/exfil beacon to 84.32.102.230:7744 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint or perimeter connections to the hardcoded attacker server 84.32.102.230 on TCP/7744, the exfil endpoint the poisoned Adform trackpoint-async.js beacons to on page load (sending victim hostname + path). This IP:port is the single highest-fidelity IOC of the campaign — it exists only in the malicious payload. Rationale: 84.32.102.230:7744 is the exact exfil IP:port confirmed across the article and second sources (BleepingComputer, Beaumont/DoublePulsar). A raw-IP non-standard-port destination with no legitimate business use makes this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/online-ad-firm-adforms-script-compromised-to-steal-cryptocurrency/ • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://blog.gridinsoft.com/adform-script-crypto-wallet-address-swap/

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / malware sandbox detonating the captured sample from a corporate range
  • Threat-intel scanners or blue-team validation traffic deliberately hitting the IOC
  • IP reallocated to a benign host after the campaign is taken down (validate against WHOIS/first-seen date)
  • Internal proxy or NAT gateway appearing as the source, collapsing many users behind one src_ip
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName in~ ("sandbox-detonation-01","malware-lab-01"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host/user and confirm the initiating process is a browser (msedge/chrome/firefox); pull the RemoteUrl/referrer the browser was on to find which affected website served the poisoned script. 2) Contain: block 84.32.102.230 at egress/firewall, and instruct the user to clear browser cache (the malicious trackpoint-async.js may persist cached) and verify any crypto wallet addresses recently copied/pasted. 3) Hunt: pivot to all hosts that both loaded s2.adform.net/banners/scripts/st/trackpoint-async.js and beaconed to this IP; alert any user who transacted crypto on July 26-27 2026.

Confirmed Adform supply-chain victim: poisoned script load + beacon to attacker IP AIDelivery High
Correlates hosts that loaded the compromised third-party resource s2.adform.net/banners/scripts/st/trackpoint-async.js with an outbound beacon to 84.32.102.230 on the same host. The script load alone is benign (Adform is loaded by thousands of legitimate sites); the join with the exfil beacon promotes it to a confirmed supply-chain compromise. Rationale: Combines the two confirmed IOCs (poisoned file path s2.adform.net/.../trackpoint-async.js and exfil IP 84.32.102.230:7744) on a single host. The join eliminates the massive benign-load noise of Adform being a legitimate ad tag, yielding a high-fidelity supply-chain-victim signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/online-ad-firm-adforms-script-compromised-to-steal-cryptocurrency/ • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1189
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Shared egress/NAT IP causes an unrelated user's script load to correlate with another user's beacon (validate on managed-host DeviceId join in Defender rather than SrcIpAddr)
  • Proxy that rewrites/caches the Adform URL so the recorded host differs from the beaconing host
  • IOC IP reallocated post-takedown to a benign service
  • Falcon variant relies on DNS to s2.adform.net which is a shared CDN host — treat DNS as a weak loader proxy, the beacon is the anchor
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each correlated host confirm the beacon process is a browser and identify the affected first-party website that embedded the tag. 2) Contain: block 84.32.102.230 at egress, force browser cache clear on the host, and reset/verify any crypto wallet addresses the user handled. 3) Hunt: enumerate every user who initiated crypto transactions during the exposure window and review outbound transfers for address substitution; notify affected clients per IR policy.

Exposure scoping: hosts that loaded poisoned Adform trackpoint-async.js (Jul 26-28 2026) AIDelivery Medium
IR-scoping hunt that surfaces every managed host which fetched s2.adform.net/banners/scripts/st/trackpoint-async.js during the compromise window (oldest malicious sample July 26, removed July 27 2026). Used to build the affected-user list for cache-clear guidance and crypto-transaction review, not as a standalone malicious-behaviour alert. Rationale: Anchored on the exact compromised resource path (s2.adform.net/.../trackpoint-async.js) and the confirmed malicious window (sample July 26, removed July 27 2026). Deliberately scoped by date because the file was benign before/after — this is an exposure list, not a malicious-behaviour detection, hence hunting tier and high expected FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/online-ad-firm-adforms-script-compromised-to-steal-cryptocurrency/ • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1189
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts that loaded the clean, restored trackpoint-async.js after Adform's July 27 fix (mitigated by the date window)
  • Legitimate marketing/ad-ops staff and QA whose job involves the Adform platform
  • Cached copies replayed after the window, skewing timestamps
  • FDR/Falcon variant keys on DNS to shared host s2.adform.net which serves many benign scripts — treat as broad exposure, not confirmation
Suppression filter
| where FirstSeen between (datetime(2026-07-26) .. datetime(2026-07-28))
Response runbook
1) Triage: treat the output as the exposed-population list; prioritise hosts/users known to handle cryptocurrency. 2) Contain: push guidance to clear browser cache (the poisoned file may remain cached) and to re-verify any wallet address before sending funds. 3) Hunt: cross-reference this list against UC 'Confirmed Adform supply-chain victim' (beacon to 84.32.102.230) to separate merely-exposed from confirmed-compromised, and review crypto transactions initiated during the window for address substitution.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp between (datetime(2026-07-26) .. datetime(2026-07-28))
| where RemoteUrl has "trackpoint-async.js" and RemoteUrl has "adform"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Hits = count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl
| order by LastSeen desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-07-26) .. datetime(2026-07-28))
| where Url has "trackpoint-async.js" and HttpHostName has "adform"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Hits = count() by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername
| order by LastSeen desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ClickFix fake-update command referencing CaptiveCrunch infrastructure · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hijacked Hotel Wi-Fi Pushes Fake Updates to Deliver Surveillance Malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] CornFlake RAT self-copy to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe · [LLM] CornFlake service registration 'svchost32' / 'Cloud Sync Service' · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Microsoft device code authentication flow phishing sign-in · [LLM] CaptiveCrunch C2 / phishing infrastructure network callback · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ChocoShell token theft from TokenBroker .tbres cache · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
CornFlake RAT self-copy to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts the CornFlake Go implant staging itself as %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe — a masquerade of the legitimate System32 svchost.exe that never legitimately lives in Roaming AppData. This is the on-disk footprint of the CaptiveCrunch implant before service registration. Rationale: Anchors on the exact implant path %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe named in Microsoft's report; the '32'-suffixed svchost in Roaming AppData is not a real Windows binary, giving near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A niche third-party 'svchost32' utility legitimately installed under Roaming (extremely rare)
  • Security researcher / malware analyst detonating a CornFlake sample in a monitored VM
  • Backup or EDR sync agent that copies quarantined samples into a Roaming staging folder
  • Custom LOB app that unfortunately named its binary svchost32.exe (validate publisher/signer)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msmpeng.exe","sense.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "Windows Defender")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull SHA256 of the created file and the InitiatingProcess; check signer status and whether the parent is a browser/terminal from a captive-portal 'update'. 2) Contain: isolate the host in Defender, kill the svchost32 process tree, and quarantine %APPDATA%\svchost32\. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'CornFlake service Cloud Sync Service' and UC 'ChocoShell Token Broker theft' on the same DeviceId; check outbound to the CaptiveCrunch C2 IOCs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "svchost32.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Roaming\svchost32\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "svchost32.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\AppData\Roaming\svchost32\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CornFlake service registration 'svchost32' / 'Cloud Sync Service' AIInstallation High
Detects registration of the CornFlake persistence service — Windows service name svchost32 with display name 'Cloud Sync Service' and description 'Synchronizes files with the cloud storage provider'. This is the service-based persistence layer of the CaptiveCrunch implant, restored by a watchdog if removed. Rationale: Uses the literal service name (svchost32), display name ('Cloud Sync Service'), and ImagePath (svchost32.exe) from Microsoft's write-up — all three are unique campaign strings, so any one match is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://www.secnews.gr/en/725008/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-xenodocheia-wifi/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate cloud-sync product coincidentally using display name 'Cloud Sync Service' (verify ImagePath is NOT svchost32.exe in Roaming)
  • EDR/backup agent re-registering a sync service after update
  • Golden-image build process installing sync services (validate against approved software list)
  • Analyst detonation of the sample in a sandbox VM
Suppression filter
| where not (ServiceFileName has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\") and ServiceFileName !has "svchost32.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm ServiceFileName resolves to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe (not a signed vendor path); note SubjectUserName that created it. 2) Contain: stop and delete the svchost32 service (sc delete), isolate host — note the watchdog will attempt restore, so remove the file drop, Run key, and scheduled task together. 3) Hunt: enumerate scheduled tasks and HKCU\...\Run entries pointing to svchost32.exe; check other travelers who used the same hotel network for the same service.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Services\svchost32"
    or (RegistryValueName =~ "DisplayName" and RegistryValueData has "Cloud Sync Service")
    or (RegistryValueName =~ "ImagePath" and RegistryValueData has "svchost32.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4697
| where ServiceName =~ "svchost32" or ServiceFileName has "svchost32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceStartType, ServiceAccount, SubjectUserName, SubjectDomainName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChocoShell token theft from TokenBroker .tbres cache AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the ChocoShell in-memory PowerShell stealer reading Microsoft 365 / Entra ID access, refresh and WAM tokens from .tbres files in the Token Broker cache. Any script interpreter (or the svchost32 implant) touching %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\TokenBroker\Cache\*.tbres is anomalous — legitimate access is by the WAM/TokenBroker host only. Rationale: Anchors on the exact artifact ChocoShell steals — .tbres files in \Microsoft\TokenBroker\Cache\ — scoped to script interpreters and the svchost32 implant; the public TBRESDecryptor tool confirms this is the real WAM/M365 token store, and normal readers are only the TokenBroker host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://github.com/shackcrack007/TBRESDecryptor
ATT&CKT1528 T1539 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A red-team/purple-team exercise running TBRESDecryptor or ROADtools
  • IT PowerShell script auditing token cache health (rare, validate signer/repo)
  • Endpoint DLP agent indexing AppData (should be its own signed process, not powershell.exe)
  • Developer debugging WAM SSO with a PowerShell helper
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\System32\", @"\Windows\SysWOW64\") and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "backgroundTaskHost.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full PowerShell command line / script block (correlate with AMSI ScriptControlScanInfo) and the acting user's UPN. 2) Contain: from Entra ID, revoke that user's refresh tokens (revokeSignInSessions) and force password + MFA re-registration; the .tbres theft yields replayable tokens without a browser. 3) Hunt: review SigninLogs/AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs for token replay from new IPs/ASNs for that user; pivot to UC 'Device code authentication flow' and the C2 IOC UC.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\Microsoft\TokenBroker\Cache\"
| where FileName endswith ".tbres"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","svchost32.exe")
    or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\AppData\Roaming\svchost32\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Microsoft\TokenBroker\Cache\"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".tbres"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","svchost32.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental

references:

#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo TargetFileName=/\\Microsoft\\TokenBroker\\Cache\\.*\.tbres$/i ContextImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh|cmd|wscript|cscript|mshta|svchost32)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId], function=count())

Microsoft device code authentication flow phishing sign-in AICommand & Control Medium
Detects successful Entra ID sign-ins that used the OAuth device code flow — the vector CaptiveCrunch landing pages have abused since 16 July to obtain MFA-satisfied, attacker-controlled sessions. Device code flow is rare in most tenants and is Microsoft's recommended Conditional-Access block, so any success is worth review. Rationale: Article states CaptiveCrunch landing pages redirect guests into Microsoft's device code flow since 16 July; device code sign-ins are the article-specific pivot and Microsoft explicitly recommends blocking them via Conditional Access, so the flow's use is inherently high-signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html
ATT&CKT1528 T1566.002
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code onboarding of IoT/CLI tools (Azure CLI 'az login --use-device-code', PowerShell Connect-AzAccount)
  • Conference-room / kiosk device provisioning
  • Developers authenticating headless apps or WSL sessions
  • Smart-TV or streaming-device Microsoft account linking
Suppression filter
| where not (AppDisplayName has_any ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell") and ConditionalAccessStatus == "success")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the IPAddress/Location and UserAgent of the device-code sign-in against the user's normal pattern and whether they were traveling; correlate the sign-in IP with the CaptiveCrunch C2 ranges. 2) Contain: revoke sessions/refresh tokens for the account and, org-wide, deploy a Conditional Access policy blocking device code flow where not required. 3) Hunt: review subsequent app consents, mailbox rules, and token replay from the same session; check other users sharing the venue/IP.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, ApplicationId, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, DeviceName, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails) has "Device Code"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed, ConditionalAccessStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CaptiveCrunch C2 / phishing infrastructure network callback AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host resolving or connecting to the confirmed CaptiveCrunch Microsoft-impersonating domains (m365-owa.com, owa-ms365.com, ms365-device.com, ms365-live.com, deltaode.com) or the four campaign C2 IPs. Covers both the fake-update/token-phishing landing pages and CornFlake implant callbacks. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the five Microsoft-impersonating domains ReliaQuest and Microsoft both documented plus the four extracted C2 IPs; exact-value matches on known-bad infrastructure are inherently high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/sandbox appliance in the org detonating the IOCs
  • Security researcher browsing the phishing domains for analysis from a sanctioned host
  • A parked/sinkholed domain reused by a benign service after takedown (validate IP still hostile)
  • DNS logging test traffic from a SOC validation run
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("SANDBOX","MALWARE-ANALYSIS","TI-DETONATE"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection — a browser suggests landing-page interaction; svchost32.exe/powershell suggests active implant C2. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block all five domains and four IPs at proxy/firewall/DNS, and add them to the TI platform. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for any historical resolution of these IOCs and pivot to the CornFlake implant-drop and Token Broker theft UCs on matching hosts.

ClickFix fake-update command referencing CaptiveCrunch infrastructure AIDelivery High
Detects the CaptiveCrunch ClickFix delivery step: a victim pastes an attacker-supplied command into a terminal/Run dialog and a script interpreter (PowerShell, cmd, mshta, curl, certutil, bitsadmin) executes with a command line that references the campaign's phishing/C2 domains or IPs. Captures the actual download cradle that pulls the fake browser/OS update. Rationale: Combines the ClickFix TTP (interpreter running a pasted command) with the campaign's specific infrastructure strings in the command line, surfacing the actual fake-update download cradle rather than a generic interpreter launch. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wifi-pushes-fake.html • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/analyst running a validation command that includes an IOC domain for testing
  • Threat-hunter pasting an IOC into a terminal while investigating
  • Sanctioned network diagnostics that curl a lookalike domain during takedown validation
  • Automated IOC sweep script that references the domains/IPs as arguments
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("IOC-sweep","threat-hunt","validate-detection"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full ProcessCommandLine to see what was downloaded/executed and identify the parent (explorer.exe = Run-dialog paste is classic ClickFix); note the user and host location. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the interpreter and any spawned installer, block the referenced IOCs. 3) Hunt: check for the CornFlake drop (%APPDATA%\svchost32\), the svchost32 service, scheduled tasks/Run keys, and Token Broker .tbres access on the same host; brief the user on captive-portal update lures.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com","ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com","deltaode.com","31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150","38.146.28.75","89.124.79.98")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com","ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com","deltaode.com","31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150","38.146.28.75","89.124.79.98")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hunts the actual exploit request for CVE-2026-53609: a PATCH to /api/v1/@apostrophecms/* whose body carries prototype-pollution keys ($pullAll, __proto__, publicApiProjection, constructor). This is the single most article-specific signal — the poisoning request that mutates Object.prototype.publicApiProjection. Rationale: Uses the exact PoC payload keys from the advisory ($pullAll, __proto__.publicApiProjection) scoped to the /api/v1/@apostrophecms/ PATCH path. Body-token match depends on WAF/proxy body logging — noted in required_telemetry. Fixed version 4.31.0 confirmed via GitLab Advisory DB and TheHackerWire. ApostropheCMS auth-bypass symptom: protected piece-type endpoint 401/403 → 200 transition AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the impact of CVE-2026-53609: a source IP that previously received 401/403 on /api/v1/@apostrophecms/user or /global begins receiving 200 responses, without any preceding successful login. This is the process-wide publicApiCheck() bypass observed on the wire. Rationale: Targets the advisory's confirmed observable: /api/v1/@apostrophecms/user and /global flipping from notfound(401/403) to a valid 200 paginated response for unauthenticated callers. Login-IP exclusion asserts the 'unauthenticated' precondition the article emphasises. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6h5j-32cf-4253 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/

Data sourcesWeb.Web

  • publicApiProjection intentionally configured on a piece-type, so unauthenticated 200s are by-design for that endpoint
  • Load balancer / uptime monitor hitting the endpoint from an IP that also fails auth elsewhere
  • CDN edge caching a 200 response and serving it to varied client IPs
Suppression filter
| where uri_path in ("/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user","/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global")

1) TRIAGE: For each flagged CIp, confirm the endpoint is one that requires auth by design (user/global) and that no successful /login/login exists for that IP; inspect whether publicApiProjection is legitimately set on the module. 2) CONTAIN: If bypass confirmed, restart the Node.js process to clear Object.prototype pollution and block the offending source IPs; upgrade to 4.31.0. 3) HUNT: Correlate the FirstSuccess timestamp backward ~minutes to find the originating PATCH with $pullAll/__proto__ (companion UC) and identify the editor account whose token performed the poisoning.
